question: M2
answer:
Current US national primary ambient air quality standards (NAAQS) for PM2.5

Short answer (as of the source retrieval date, 2026-11-16):
1. Primary annual PM2.5 standard: 9.0 µg/m³ (annual arithmetic mean concentration).
2. Primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard: 35 µg/m³ (24-hour average concentration).

Regulatory basis and status
- The operative codified primary PM2.5 NAAQS are at 40 CFR 50.20, added by the final reconsideration rule published at 89 FR 16380 (Mar. 6, 2024), effective May 6, 2024. Section 50.20(a) states the standards are 9.0 µg/m³ annual arithmetic mean and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour average. Section 50.20(b) provides the annual standard is met at ≤ 9.0 µg/m³; §50.20(c) provides the 24-hour standard is met at ≤ 35 µg/m³.
- EPA's Feb. 7, 2024 final reconsideration announcement states EPA set the primary annual PM2.5 standard at 9.0 µg/m³ and did not change the primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard. The 24-hour level therefore remains 35 µg/m³, carried over from the 2012/2013 PM NAAQS review (78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013).
- Historical/do-not-use: 40 CFR 50.18 displays the prior primary annual level of 12.0 µg/m³ from the 2013 rule. That is the superseded annual level, not the current one. Some mirrors or caches may still show it; the current 2024 codification is §50.20 with 9.0 µg/m³.

Form of the standards (so the levels are not misread)
- Annual: annual arithmetic mean concentration, averaged over 3 years as specified in appendix N; compared to 9.0 µg/m³.
- 24-hour: 98th percentile of 24-hour concentrations, averaged over 3 years as specified in appendix N; compared to 35 µg/m³.
- 'Primary' means the health-based standard under Clean Air Act §109, not the welfare-based secondary standard.

Do not conflate
- Secondary (welfare-based) annual PM2.5 standard is 15.0 µg/m³, and secondary 24-hour is 35 µg/m³; these are not the requested primary values.
- PM10 standards (for example, primary 24-hour PM10 of 150 µg/m³) are separate and not part of this answer.

Sources checked
- 40 CFR 50.20 (eCFR current text, fetched 2026-11-16): 9.0 µg/m³ annual and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour; 89 FR 16380.
- EPA, Final Reconsideration of the NAAQS for PM (Feb. 7, 2024): primary annual set at 9.0 µg/m³; 24-hour not changed.
- 40 CFR 50.18 (eCFR): prior 2013 text showing 12.0 µg/m³ annual; identified as historical/superseded, not current.

question: M4
answer:
ANSWER

4 feet (1.2 m) above a lower level.

A US employer in general industry must protect an employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge from falling when that surface is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level.

GOVERNING TEXT

29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) (Walking-Working Surfaces, Subpart D), current federal text:

  "Except as provided elsewhere in this section, the employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following:
    (A) Guardrail systems;
    (B) Safety net systems; or
    (C) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems."

Key points of construction:
- The trigger is 4 ft "or more" measured from the walking-working surface down to the lower level. At exactly 4.0 ft the duty attaches; below 4.0 ft this paragraph does not compel fall protection.
- "Unprotected side or edge" is defined in 1910.28/1910.21 as any side or edge of a walking-working surface (except at entrances and other points of access) where there is no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system protecting the employee from falling to a lower level. A parapet or wall of adequate height therefore removes the trigger.
- "Walking-working surface" is any horizontal or vertical surface on or through which an employee walks, works, or gains access to a work area or workplace location.
- The duty is to provide one or more of the three listed systems; the employer chooses among guardrail, safety net, or personal fall protection (the standard does not mandate a single hierarchy, though the note to (b)(1)(ii) presumes feasibility of at least one listed system).
- Corroborating general-industry text at the same 4 ft figure: 1910.28(b)(15) ("Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed ... 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level") and 1910.28(b)(14)(i) (slaughtering facility platforms, 4 feet (1.2 m) or more).

SCOPE CONFIRMATION AND WHAT THIS FIGURE IS NOT

- Industry: general industry, 29 CFR Part 1910, Subpart D. Correct answer: 4 ft.
- Not construction: 29 CFR 1926.501(b)(1) uses 6 ft for construction work. That 6 ft figure must not be carried into a general-industry walking-working surface analysis. (Stated only as a contrast; it is not the answer.)
- Not shipyard (1910.140 / Subpart F historically 5 ft), not longshoring (1917), not agriculture (1928). Different parts, different numbers.
- Effective date: the current 1910.28 framework took effect January 17, 2017 (with phase-ins for specific provisions). Pre-2017 general-industry citations to former 1910.23 gave 4 ft for open-sided floors and platforms, so the 4 ft answer is stable across the revision for this particular question, but the paragraph numbering changed — cite 1910.28(b)(1)(i), not former 1910.23(c)(1), in anything written today.

EXCEPTIONS AND OVERLAYS THAT DISPLACE OR MODIFY THE GENERAL 4 FT RULE

The paragraph opens "Except as provided elsewhere in this section," so the following must be checked before resting on 4 ft:

1. Low-slope roofs — 1910.28(b)(13). This is a distance-from-edge overlay, not a different height trigger. Work less than 6 ft (1.6 m) from the roof edge requires guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest. Work 6 ft to less than 15 ft (4.6 m) from the edge requires one of those systems, or a designated area if the work is infrequent and temporary. Work 15 ft or more from the edge requires one of those systems or a designated area, and no fall protection is required if the work is both infrequent and temporary. Note the practical effect: on a low-slope roof, proximity to the edge — not the 4 ft height — drives the requirement.
2. Holes — 1910.28(b)(3) imposes a separate duty for holes (including skylights) at the same 4 ft figure, plus covers and guardrails for holes through which objects can fall. Verify current text before quoting.
3. Ramps, stairways, dockboards, rope descent systems, ladders, and outdoor advertising structures each have their own paragraph in 1910.28(b). Rope descent systems expressly retain 4 ft (1910.28(b)(12)(ii): employee 4 ft or more above a lower level protected by personal fall arrest). Fixed ladders carry their own 24 ft-related provisions and phase-in dates — re-verify against the current eCFR before citing a specific number; do not assume 4 ft governs fixed-ladder climbing.
4. Feasibility exceptions. 1910.28(b)(1)(ii) (residential roofs) and 1910.28(b)(1)(iii) (loading rack, loading dock, teeming platform working side) permit work without a fall protection system where the employer can demonstrate infeasibility, the work operation is in process, access is limited to authorized employees, and those employees are trained per 1910.30. The note to (b)(1)(ii) places the burden on the employer: there is a presumption that at least one listed system is feasible and will not create a greater hazard.
5. Other subparts. 1910.28(b)(1)(i) is also subject to carve-outs listed at the start of 1910.28(a) — powered platforms (1910.66(j)), aerial lifts (1910.67(c)(2)(v)), telecommunications (1910.268(n)(7)-(8)), and electric power generation/transmission/distribution (1910.269(g)(2)(i)).

JURISDICTION

Federal OSHA (29 CFR 1910.28) governs in states without an OSHA-approved State Plan. State-Plan states must be at least as effective as federal OSHA and may differ. Verified example: Oregon OSHA's Division 2, Subdivision D reproduces 1910.28(b)(1)(i) with the same 4 feet (1.2 m) figure (Oregon did not adopt (b)(1)(ii) or its note). Before relying on 4 ft for a specific site in a State-Plan state (e.g., California, Washington, Michigan, Oregon), confirm that state's adopted text; the figure is commonly identical, but the exceptions and the roof provisions are where state plans diverge.

MEANS OF PROTECTION — DIMENSIONAL CHECK (so the chosen system actually satisfies the duty)

Guardrail systems under 1910.29(b): top rail 42 inches (107 cm) plus or minus 3 inches (8 cm) above the walking-working surface; top edge may exceed 45 inches (114 cm) if all other criteria are met; midrail, screen, mesh, or equivalent intermediate member installed where there is no wall or parapet at least 21 inches (53 cm) high. These are guardrail geometry requirements, not fall-protection triggers, and do not alter the 4 ft answer.

PRACTICAL DECISION PROCEDURE

1. Confirm general industry (Part 1910) rather than construction (Part 1926) or a maritime part.
2. Confirm the state is federal OSHA or check the State Plan's adopted text.
3. Identify the walking-working surface and the lower level; measure vertical distance. If 4 ft (1.2 m) or more and the side/edge has no wall, guardrail, or stair rail, the duty attaches.
4. Check 1910.28(b)(2)-(15) and 1910.28(a) carve-outs for a more specific provision (especially low-slope roofs, holes, fixed ladders, rope descent). The specific provision controls.
5. Select one or more of guardrail, safety net, or personal fall protection; design/install to 1910.29 and 1910.30 (training) and 1910.140 (personal fall protection systems).
6. If invoking an infeasibility exception, document the demonstration, limit access to authorized employees, keep it to the work in progress, and train per 1910.30 — the burden of proof is the employer's.

VERIFICATION STATUS OF CITED NUMBERS

Directly supported by the retrieved regulatory text: 4 ft (1.2 m) at 1910.28(b)(1)(i), (b)(14)(i), (b)(15); 6 ft and 15 ft distance-from-edge bands at 1910.28(b)(13); 4 ft for rope descent at (b)(12)(ii); guardrail 42 in +/- 3 in and 21 in parapet at 1910.29(b). Items flagged "re-verify" (holes, fixed ladders, other (b) paragraphs) are stated qualitatively or with an explicit verification flag and are not relied on for the answer.

question: M6
answer:
ANSWER

Under 14 CFR Part 91, a helicopter (legally, a rotorcraft) beginning a VFR flight in the United States must carry, in addition to the fuel needed to fly to the first point of intended landing, enough fuel to fly for at least 20 minutes at normal cruising speed. This 20-minute reserve is the same for day and night VFR — there is no separate night figure for rotorcraft.

Controlling regulation, 14 CFR 91.151(b), verbatim:

  'No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.'

STRUCTURE OF THE REQUIREMENT

1. Fuel to the first point of intended landing, computed considering wind and forecast weather conditions. This is not a no-wind still-air number; the regulation explicitly requires wind and forecast to be taken into account.
2. Plus 20 minutes at normal cruising speed — this is the reserve, and it is measured in time, not in gallons or pounds.
3. No alternate-airport fuel is required for VFR. The alternate fuel requirement lives in the IFR rules (91.167(a)(2), 135.223(a)(2)) and has no VFR counterpart. A VFR flight plan does not require a filed alternate.

WHAT DOES NOT APPLY (common sources of error)

- Airplane day/night split: 91.151(a) requires 30 minutes by day and 45 minutes at night, but that paragraph applies to airplanes only. Using 30 or 45 for a helicopter overstates the legal minimum (conservative, but wrong as an answer to the question).
- Night penalty: the airplane 45-minute night figure does not transfer to rotorcraft. 91.151(b) contains no day/night distinction; 20 minutes applies around the clock.
- IFR: 91.167(a)(3) requires helicopters to carry 30 minutes at normal cruising speed after the alternate (or after the destination if no alternate is required). That is a different regime; a helicopter flying VFR needs 20 minutes, not 30.
- Part 135: if the flight is conducted commercially under Part 135, 135.209(b) independently requires 'at least 20 minutes' for helicopters under VFR, day or night. The number is identical to Part 91, so the Part 91 vs. Part 135 ambiguity does not change the answer for a helicopter. (Part 135 airplanes differ: 30 min day / 45 min night under 135.209(a).)
- Part 121 and Part 125 are airplane-centric and not the governing framework for a typical helicopter VFR flight.

SCOPE NOTES

- The rule says 'rotorcraft,' which covers helicopters and gyroplanes. A powered-lift certificated under the Part 194 framework may use the rotorcraft/helicopter VFR fuel minimums when it has the performance capability to complete the flight and land in the vertical-lift flight mode (FAA AC 194-1, discussion of 135.209 and 194.306(ss)); in wing-borne mode it must use airplane criteria.
- The 20 minutes is a regulatory floor, not a flight-planning target. 14 CFR 91.103 requires the pilot in command to become familiar with all available information concerning the flight, including fuel required, and known traffic delays or other conditions must be accounted for. Operator manuals, OpSpecs, and company fuel policies commonly set higher minimums, and those govern when they are more restrictive.
- The 20 minutes is measured against usable fuel. Fuel that cannot be used in flight (unusable fuel per the rotorcraft flight manual, or fuel in a tank that cannot be fed to the engine in the planned configuration) does not count toward either the en-route fuel or the reserve.

CONVERTING 20 MINUTES TO A QUANTITY

Reserve quantity = (20 / 60) x normal cruise fuel flow = (1/3) x cruise fuel flow, using the fuel flow at the speed the flight will actually be conducted at (normal cruising speed), in the same units as the fuel gauges and the flight manual.

Worked examples:
- Cruise fuel flow 12 gal/h: reserve = 12 x 20/60 = 4.0 gal.
- Cruise fuel flow 15 gal/h: reserve = 15 x 20/60 = 5.0 gal.
- Cruise fuel flow 160 lb/h: reserve = 160 x 20/60 = 53.3 lb.
- Cruise fuel flow 60 L/h: reserve = 60 x 20/60 = 20 L.

Total fuel at start of flight must therefore be at least: (fuel to first point of intended landing, wind-adjusted) + (1/3 x cruise fuel flow) + (any taxi/run-up/start allowance the operator's procedure adds) + (unusable fuel, if the operator's convention tracks total rather than usable quantity).

ONE-LINE ANSWER

20 minutes of flying time at normal cruising speed, in addition to the wind-adjusted fuel required to reach the first point of intended landing — the same 20 minutes whether the flight is by day or by night, and the same 20 minutes under either Part 91 or Part 135 for a helicopter.

The first reads: "VerDate Sep<11>2014 10:01 Aug 27, 2026 Jkt 268049 PO 00000 Frm 00484 Fmt 8010 Sfmt 8002 Y:\SGML\268049.XXX 268049jgilmore on DSK4WB1RN3PROD with CFR"

The first reads: "(1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes;"

Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 45 on ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-i/subchapter-g/part-135/subpart-d and 20 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/cfr-2026-title14-vol2/pdf/cfr-2026-title14-vol2-part91.pdf. The first reads: "(2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes."

question: M8
answer:
ANSWERS

1. The RFC that deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 is RFC 8996, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1" (K. Moriarty, S. Farrell), published March 2021. It is an Internet Best Current Practice and is part of BCP 195 (it updates RFC 7525, the previous BCP 195 document).

2. The status it gave to the RFCs that defined those protocol versions — RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) and RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1) — is Historic. RFC 8996 moved both documents to Historic status.

VERBATIM SUPPORT (RFC 8996 abstract, identical across the HTML, info-page, XML and inline-errata renderings at rfc-editor.org, and reproduced in the Datatracker record):

  "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS)
   versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346).  Accordingly, those
   documents have been moved to Historic status."

And in Section 1 (Introduction):

  "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1
   [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has now
   itself been superseded by TLS 1.3 [RFC8446]. ... Therefore, it is
   timely to further deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0.
   Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic
   status."

PRECISION NOTES (important distinctions, stated so the answer is not misread)

- "Moved to Historic" is a change of document status in the RFC index; it is not the same as obsoletion. RFC 8996 does not list RFC 2246 or RFC 4346 in its Obsoletes header. The Datatracker/RFC metadata for RFC 8996 records obsoletes: RFC 5469, RFC 7507 only. RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 are recorded as Historic.
- RFC 8996's own status is Best Current Practice (BCP 195), not Historic. It is the deprecating document, not a deprecated one.
- The same document also moved DTLS 1.0 (RFC 4347) and RFC 5469 to Historic, and it deprecates TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1 and DTLS 1.0 while explicitly not deprecating DTLS 1.2 (there is no DTLS 1.1). It updates a long list of RFCs that normatively reference TLS 1.0/1.1 (e.g., RFC 3261, RFC 3329, RFC 3436, RFC 3501, RFC 3552, RFC 4513, RFC 5246-adjacent profiles, RFC 6347, RFC 7525, RFC 8422, among many others).
- The deprecation rationale given in Section 1: these versions require implementing cipher suites no longer desirable (e.g., TLS 1.0 makes TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA mandatory to implement), lack support for AEAD cipher suites (not available before TLS 1.2), depend on SHA-1 for handshake integrity and for peer authentication signatures, and increase implementation attack surface and misconfiguration risk.

AUTHORITATIVE SOURCES

- RFC 8996 text: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8996.html (also .xml, .txt, .pdf; DOI 10.17487/RFC8996)
- RFC 8996 index/metadata: https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8996/ (status: Best Current Practice; part of BCP 195; March 2021)
- Publication history: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8996/history/ (draft-ietf-tls-oldversions-deprecate-00 through -12; RFC 8996 published 2021-03-23)
- Inline errata rendering confirming the abstract text: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/inline-errata/rfc8996.html

ONE-LINE ANSWER

RFC 8996 ("Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1", BCP 195, March 2021) deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 and moved their defining RFCs — RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 — to Historic status.

question: M10
answer:
ANSWER

The US Social Security contribution and benefit base (the OASDI taxable maximum — the most earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax) for calendar year 2026 is $184,500.

1. VALUE AND SCOPE
- Figure: $184,500 (US dollars, calendar year 2026).
- Program: Old-Age, Survivors, and Disability Insurance (OASDI) only. Medicare (HI) has no wage base limit — all covered wages are subject to the 1.45%/1.45% Medicare tax regardless of the base.
- Meaning: earnings up to $184,500 in 2026 are subject to the 6.2% employee and 6.2% employer Social Security tax; earnings above that amount are not taxed for OASDI. The same $184,500 is the maximum amount of 2026 earnings that can be credited toward a Social Security benefit computation.
- This is the officially determined figure, not a projection. It appears on SSA's automatic-determination tables and in IRS Pub. 15 (2026), so it is in force for tax year 2026.

2. SOURCE VERIFICATION (four independent, mutually consistent sources)
- SSA, "Automatic Determinations in Recent Years" (ssa.gov/oact/cola/autoAdj.html): 2026 row — COLA 3.6%, contribution and benefit base $184,500. Neighboring rows: 2025 = $176,100; 2027 = $192,300.
- SSA, "Contribution and Benefit Base" (ssa.gov/oact/COLA/cbb.html): historical table, 2026 = 184,500; 2027 = 192,300.
- IRS Publication 15 (2026), Catalog No. 10000W, dated Dec 15, 2025: "The social security wage base limit is $184,500"; and "For 2026, the social security tax rate is 6.2% ... each for the employer and employee (12.4% total). ... There is no wage base limit for Medicare tax."
- SSA Publication No. 42-007, EFW2 Tax Year 2026 (11/12/2026): Social Security Wages/Tips fields must not exceed "the annual maximum Social Security wage base for the tax year ($184,500 for tax year 2026)"; Social Security Tax Withheld must not exceed $11,439.00.
All four agree; there is no conflicting figure in the record. The value is explicitly distinguished from the 2025 figure ($176,100), the prior-year value that is the usual source of error.

3. INTERNAL CONSISTENCY CHECKS (arithmetic against the stated limits)
- Employee maximum OASDI tax: 6.2% x $184,500 = $11,439.00 — exactly the EFW2 2026 Social Security Tax Withheld ceiling. Consistent.
- Combined employer + employee: 12.4% x $184,500 = $22,878.00.
- Self-employed (SECA) OASDI: 12.4% x $184,500 = $22,878.00.
- Ordering check: $176,100 (2025) < $184,500 (2026) < $192,300 (2027). Monotonic, as required by the no-reduction clause of the statute.

4. STATUTORY DETERMINATION RECOMPUTED (independent confirmation of the $184,500)
Method (Social Security Act, as summarized on SSA's cbbdet page): base for year Y after 1994 = 1994 base of $60,600 x [national average wage index for year (Y-2) / national average wage index for 1992], rounded to the nearest multiple of $300; never reduced below the prior year's base.
For Y = 2026, the index year is 2024:
- 1994 base = $60,600
- 1992 average wage index = 22,935.42
- 2024 average wage index = 69,846.57
- Ratio = 69,846.57 / 22,935.42 = 3.045358
- $60,600 x 3.045358 = $184,548.7
- Round to nearest $300: 184,548.7 / 300 = 615.16 -> 615 x 300 = $184,500 (candidate) vs. 616 x 300 = $184,800; |184,548.7 - 184,500| = 48.7 < |184,800 - 184,548.7| = 251.3, so the nearest multiple is $184,500.
- $184,500 > 2025 base of $176,100, so the no-reduction floor does not apply.
Result: $184,500. This reproduces the published figure exactly.

CAUTION ON A LOOK-ALIKE COMPUTATION: SSA's cbbdet page currently shows the 2027 determination, which uses the 2025 average wage index (72,800.33) and yields $192,300. That computation is for 2027, not 2026. The 2026 figure derives from the 2024 average wage index (69,846.57) and yields $184,500. Do not substitute the 2027 arithmetic or the 2027 value for the 2026 answer.

5. ADJACENT 2026 FIGURES (for context only; not part of the answer)
- Medicare (HI) taxable maximum: none — no cap in 2026.
- Additional Medicare Tax threshold (0.9%): $200,000 single / $250,000 joint — a separate provision, not the contribution and benefit base.
- 2026 retirement earnings test: $24,480 (under full retirement age, $1 withheld per $2 over); $65,160 (year of full retirement age, $1 per $3 over); no limit at or after full retirement age.
- 2026 coverage credit: $1,890 of earnings per credit; four credits maximum per year.
- 2026 COLA: 3.6%.

6. BOTTOM LINE
$184,500 for 2026.

question: M12
answer:
2026 ELECTIVE DEFERRAL LIMIT — 401(k), EXCLUDING CATCH-UP

ANSWER
$24,500.

The limit on an employee's elective deferrals (traditional pre-tax and designated Roth combined) to a 401(k) plan for the 2026 calendar year, before any catch-up contribution, is $24,500. It is also capped at 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less.

AUTHORITY
- IRS Notice 2025-67 (2026 cost-of-living adjustments): the §402(g)(1) limitation on the exclusion for elective deferrals 'is increased from $23,500 to $24,500.'
- IRS, Retirement Topics — 401(k) and Profit-Sharing Plan Contribution Limits: '$24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments.'
- IRS Publication 560: 'The limit on elective deferrals, other than catch-up contributions, is $23,500 for 2025 and $24,500 for 2026.'
This is a published figure for 2026, not a projection.

WHAT THE $24,500 DOES AND DOES NOT COVER
- Applies per employee, but is aggregated across plans. An employee who defers to more than one 401(k), plus any 403(b) or governmental 457(b), must total all of those elective deferrals against the single $24,500 §402(g) limit for the year. (A governmental 457(b) has its own separate §457(e)(15) limit, which is also $24,500 for 2026.)
- Traditional and Roth deferrals share the one limit; electing Roth does not create extra room.
- Catch-up contributions sit outside the limit:
  • Age 50+ (including ages 60-63): $8,000 for 2026.
  • SECURE 2.0 higher catch-up for participants who attain age 60, 61, 62, or 63 in 2026: $11,250.
  • Maximum deferral for 2026 including catch-up: $24,500 + $8,000 = $32,500; or $24,500 + $11,250 = $35,750 for the age 60-63 group.
- This is not the total-contribution limit. The §415(c) annual additions limit for 2026 is $72,000 (plus catch-up), covering employee deferrals plus employer match, nonelective contributions, and forfeiture allocations. $24,500 is a sub-limit inside that ceiling.
- Not the SIMPLE 401(k) limit. A SIMPLE 401(k) deferral limit for 2026 is $17,000 (plus catch-up), not $24,500.
- Not the §401(a)(17) compensation cap. Compensation taken into account for plan purposes is capped at $360,000 for 2026.

HR OPERATIONAL NOTES
1. Payroll system configuration: set the 2026 pre-tax + Roth deferral annual cap at $24,500 and set the catch-up cap separately ($8,000, or $11,250 where the participant attains 60-63 in 2026 and the plan permits the higher amount). Do not net catch-up against the $24,500.
2. Plan terms can be stricter, never looser. A plan document may impose a lower deferral percentage or dollar cap, and highly compensated employees may have deferrals limited or refunded to pass ADP/ACP nondiscrimination testing. The IRS limit is a ceiling, not an entitlement.
3. Multi-plan employees: obtain a deferral election/attestation from any employee who also participates in another employer's 401(k), a 403(b), or a governmental 457(b). Excess §402(g) deferrals must generally be distributed (with allocable earnings) by April 15 of the following year to avoid double taxation; the employee bears the tax on the excess.
4. Off-calendar plan years: §402(g) operates on the calendar year for the individual, even if the plan year differs. Short plan years do not prorate the $24,500.
5. Communicate the number as '$24,500 for 2026' and pair it with the catch-up figures so employees age 50+ are not misinformed about their own maximum.

SCOPE / CAVEATS
Stated for US federal tax law, USD, §402(g) employee elective deferrals to a 401(k). It does not address plan-specific caps, nondiscrimination-test outcomes, state tax treatment, 403(b)/457(b) special rules in detail, or the §415(c) total-contribution calculation beyond the $72,000 ceiling noted above. If the request was instead for a SIMPLE 401(k), the figure is $17,000; if it was for total annual additions, the figure is $72,000.

question: M2
answer:
## Current US national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5

**As-of basis:** eCFR current text of 40 CFR Part 50, fetched 2026-11-16. The current primary PM2.5 standards are codified at **40 CFR §50.20**, added by the 2024 PM2.5 NAAQS final rule (89 FR 16380, Mar. 6, 2024).

| Ask | Standard | Level | Unit | Statistical form / averaging | Citation |
|---|---|---:|---|---|---|
| 1 | Primary annual PM2.5 | **9.0** | µg/m³ | Annual arithmetic mean concentration, as determined under 40 CFR Part 50, Appendix N; met when the annual arithmetic mean is ≤ 9.0 µg/m³. Appendix N uses a 3-year average of annual arithmetic means. | 40 CFR §50.20(a), (b) |
| 2 | Primary 24-hour PM2.5 | **35** | µg/m³ | 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, as determined under 40 CFR Part 50, Appendix N; met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration is ≤ 35 µg/m³. Appendix N uses a 3-year average of annual 98th-percentile 24-hour concentrations. | 40 CFR §50.20(a), (c) |

### Authoritative text

40 CFR §50.20(a) states that the national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are:

> “9.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m3) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m3 24-hour average concentration …”

Section §50.20(b) provides that the primary annual PM2.5 standard is met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, as determined in accordance with Appendix N, is less than or equal to **9.0 µg/m³**. Section §50.20(c) provides that the primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard is met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, as determined in accordance with Appendix N, is less than or equal to **35 µg/m³**.

### Important regulatory note on the older 12.0 µg/m³ value

40 CFR §50.18 still recites the 2012 primary PM2.5 standards: **12.0 µg/m³ annual** and **35 µg/m³ 24-hour** (78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013). The **12.0 µg/m³ annual value is not the current annual primary standard**; it is the older annual level. The current annual primary level is **9.0 µg/m³** under §50.20. The 24-hour primary level remains **35 µg/m³** and appears in both §50.18 and §50.20 because it was retained in the 2024 review.

### Scope

This answer covers the **federal primary (health-based) NAAQS for PM2.5** under the Clean Air Act. It does not cover secondary (welfare-based) PM2.5 standards, state or local standards, or non-US standards. The secondary annual PM2.5 standard is a different value (15.0 µg/m³) and should not be substituted for the primary annual level requested here.

question: M6
answer:
# VFR Reserve Fuel Requirement — Helicopter, United States

## 1. Answer

**20 minutes.** A helicopter may not begin a VFR flight in the United States unless it carries enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, after that point, to fly for at least **20 minutes at normal cruising speed / normal cruising fuel consumption**. This is the reserve that must be on board *in addition to* trip fuel to the first landing point.

The 20-minute figure applies **day or night** — there is no day/night split for helicopters under VFR. It is the same under the general operating rules (Part 91) and under Part 135 helicopter operations.

## 2. Regulatory basis (primary text, as retrieved)

**14 CFR §91.151 Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions, paragraph (b):**

> "(b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

**14 CFR §135.209 VFR: Fuel supply, paragraph (b):**

> "(b) No person may begin a flight operation in a helicopter under VFR unless, considering wind and forecast weather conditions, it has enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising fuel consumption, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes."

**Corroborating FAA handbook excerpt** (FAA fuel-planning guidance document, item "19. FAR PART 91 HELICOPTER VFR CONDITIONS" and item "15. FAR PART 135 HELICOPTER VFR OPERATIONS"):

> "Reserve Fuel. FAR §91.151(b). During day or night the required reserve fuel is the amount that allows continued operation for 20 minutes."

> "Reserve Fuel. FAR §135.209(b). During day or night the required reserve fuel is the amount that allows continued operation for 20 minutes."

Sources retrieved and used:
- eCFR, 14 CFR Part 91 Subpart B, §91.151 (fetched 2026-11-16, sha256 a8a7e00944fb)
- GovInfo, CFR 2026 title 14 vol 2, Part 91 (sha256 ba317cd8bb4c)
- eCFR, 14 CFR Part 135 Subpart D (sha256 3bc146dfae5b)
- GovInfo, CFR 2026 title 14 vol 3, §135.209 (sha256 b1aa75d389a0)
- FAA fuel-planning guidance, faa.gov/media/32056 (sha256 eee9cbe139d5)

**Excluded source:** a New Zealand Civil Aviation Authority Part 91 page (aviation.govt.nz, rule 91.305(b)) also states a 20-minute helicopter VFR reserve. It was retrieved by the search but is **not** US law and forms no part of this answer. Its coincidental agreement with the US figure is not evidence for the US figure.

## 3. Why day/night does not change the answer for helicopters

The day/night distinction exists only in the **airplane** paragraphs. Do not import it:

| Category / rule | Day | Night |
|---|---|---|
| Airplane, VFR, §91.151(a) | 30 min | 45 min |
| Airplane, VFR, §135.209(a) | 30 min | 45 min |
| **Helicopter/rotorcraft, VFR, §91.151(b)** | **20 min** | **20 min** |
| **Helicopter, VFR, §135.209(b)** | **20 min** | **20 min** |

The bolded rows are the answer. The airplane rows are shown only to explain the common 30/45 error.

## 4. Part 91 vs Part 135 — the operating-part question is moot here

A frequent failure mode is answering the wrong operating part. For VFR helicopters it does not matter: Part 91 §91.151(b) and Part 135 §135.209(b) both require **20 minutes**. Confirm the operating part anyway, because it changes other things (e.g., §135.213 weather-source requirements), but the reserve number is 20 minutes either way. If the flight is neither (public aircraft, military), the applicable service rule governs and is outside this answer.

## 5. What the reserve is measured in, and how to turn it into a fuel quantity

The regulation is written in **time**, not gallons or pounds. The reserve is therefore:

- **20 minutes of flight time**, computed at **normal cruising speed** (§91.151(b)) / **normal cruising fuel consumption** (§135.209(b)).
- Normal cruising speed/consumption means the speed and burn the flight is actually planned at — not max range, not hover, not a max-continuous-power figure.

**Conversion formulas:**

- Reserve volume (US gal) = (normal-cruise burn rate in gal/hr) × (20 ÷ 60) = burn rate ÷ 3
- Reserve mass (lb) = (normal-cruise burn rate in lb/hr) × (20 ÷ 60) = burn rate ÷ 3
- Reserve still-air distance (NM) = (normal-cruise TAS in kt) × (20 ÷ 60) = TAS ÷ 3

**Worked example:** normal cruise burn 24 gal/hr, cruise TAS 110 kt.
- Reserve = 24 ÷ 3 = **8.0 US gal**
- Reserve distance equivalent = 110 ÷ 3 = **36.7 NM**
- Minimum fuel at brake release = trip fuel to first landing point (computed with forecast wind) + 8.0 gal + any contingency fuel for known delays (§91.103)

Use **usable** fuel only. Unusable fuel, fuel that cannot be fed in the planned attitude, and fuel below a run-tank/limitation quantity do not count toward the 20 minutes.

## 6. Scope boundaries — what the 20 minutes does and does not cover

- **It is a floor, not a target.** It is the regulatory minimum. Operators, employers, and OEMs routinely impose higher internal minimums; those govern the flight if higher.
- **No alternate fuel is required for VFR.** Alternate-airport fuel (e.g., §91.169) is an IFR construct. The VFR reserve is a single 20-minute block, not trip fuel plus alternate plus reserve.
- **Contingency fuel is separate.** §91.103 preflight action requires accounting for known traffic delays and other information affecting the flight. That fuel sits on top of the 20-minute reserve, not inside it.
- **IFR helicopters are different.** Under §91.167(a)(3) and §135.223(a)(3), a helicopter in IFR conditions must carry fuel to fly after the approach/alternate sequence for **30 minutes** at normal cruising speed. That 30-minute figure must **not** be used for a VFR flight, and the 20-minute figure must not be used for an IFR flight.
- **"Begin a flight"** — §91.151 is a prohibition on beginning the flight without the fuel. The check is at brake release / start of the flight, using forecast wind and weather. Tailwinds that shorten the trip do not reduce the 20-minute reserve, and headwinds do not excuse it.
- **State, local, and airport rules** may add requirements (e.g., fuel requirements for certain airspace or operators). They can only make the requirement more restrictive, never less.

## 7. Verification procedure (confirm before relying on the number)

1. Open eCFR Title 14, Part 91, Subpart B, §91.151 (and Part 135 Subpart D, §135.209 if operating under Part 135).
2. Confirm the retrieved text is current: check the eCFR "current as of" date and the amendment history line under the section.
3. Read the paragraph for the correct category — **rotorcraft** in §91.151(b), **helicopter** in §135.209(b). Do not read paragraph (a).
4. Confirm the flight is VFR. If IFR, switch to §91.167/§135.223 and use 30 minutes for helicopters.
5. Confirm no exemption, deviation, or operations-specification provision modifies the requirement for the specific operator.
6. Convert to a fuel quantity using the aircraft's normal-cruise burn from its performance data (POH/RFMS), and confirm the resulting quantity is usable.

## 8. Common errors this answer is designed to pre-empt

| Wrong answer | Why it is wrong |
|---|---|
| 30 minutes (day) / 45 minutes (night) | Those are **airplane** VFR reserves under §91.151(a)/§135.209(a). |
| 30 minutes | That is the **helicopter IFR** reserve under §91.167(a)(3)/§135.223(a)(3). |
| 45 minutes | Airplane IFR reserve. |
| A fixed gallon figure | The rule is in time; gallons depend on the individual aircraft's cruise burn. |
| "20 minutes total fuel" | 20 minutes is the **reserve beyond** fuel to the first point of intended landing, per the request's framing. |
| 20 minutes adjusted for day/night | No day/night split exists for helicopters under VFR. |

## 9. Bottom line

**20 minutes** of flight time at normal cruising speed, carried in addition to fuel to reach the first point of intended landing, day or night, under either Part 91 (§91.151(b)) or Part 135 (§135.209(b)). Convert to quantity as normal-cruise burn rate ÷ 3.

The first reads: "(1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes;"

Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 45 on ecfr.gov/current/title-14/chapter-i/subchapter-g/part-135/subpart-d and 20 on govinfo.gov/content/pkg/cfr-2026-title14-vol2/pdf/cfr-2026-title14-vol2-part91.pdf. The first reads: "(2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes."

# Deprecation of TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 — RFC identification and assigned status

## Direct answers

1. **The RFC that deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 is RFC 8996**, *Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1* (K. Moriarty, S. Farrell; March 2021; part of BCP 195; status: Best Current Practice).
2. **It assigned those defining documents the status "Historic".** RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) and RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1) were **moved to Historic status**. The same treatment was applied to RFC 4347 (DTLS 1.0), and RFC 5469 was also moved to Historic; RFC 7507 was marked as superseded (both are listed in RFC 8996's `obsoletes` metadata).

## Supporting quotations (RFC 8996, verbatim)

From the Abstract:

> "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."

From Section 1 (Introduction):

> "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has now itself been superseded by TLS 1.3 [RFC8446]. ... Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status."

From the Abstract, on scope beyond the two protocols asked about:

> "This document also deprecates Datagram TLS (DTLS) version 1.0 (RFC 4347) but not DTLS version 1.2, and there is no DTLS version 1.1."

## Mapping table

| Item | RFC | Role | Status after RFC 8996 |
|---|---|---|---|
| TLS 1.0 specification | RFC 2246 | Defined TLS 1.0 | **Historic** |
| TLS 1.1 specification | RFC 4346 | Defined TLS 1.1 | **Historic** |
| Deprecating document | **RFC 8996** | Formally deprecates TLS 1.0 and 1.1 | Best Current Practice (part of BCP 195) |

## Two distinctions worth keeping straight

- **The deprecating document's own status is not "Historic."** RFC 8996's "Status of This Memo" reads: "This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice." Its IANA/RFC Editor publication status is `BEST CURRENT PRACTICE`. "Historic" is the status it *assigned to* RFC 2246 and RFC 4346, not its own.
- **"Moved to Historic" is a status change, not an obsoletion.** RFC 8996's `obsoletes` list contains RFC 5469 and RFC 7507 only; RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 are not obsoleted by it. They had already been superseded on the standards track by RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2, 2008) and RFC 8446 (TLS 1.3, 2018); RFC 8996 changed their status to Historic and updated the many RFCs that normatively referenced TLS 1.0/1.1.

## Practical reading

An implementation or policy statement citing this deprecation should say: *TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 are deprecated by RFC 8996 (BCP 195, March 2021), which moved their defining specifications, RFC 2246 and RFC 4346, to Historic status; TLS 1.2 or later is required.* This is the IETF-level statement; product- or regime-specific prohibitions (for example, payment-card or government profiles referenced in RFC 8996's rationale) are separate authorities and are not themselves the answer to this question.

ANSWER

The US Social Security contribution and benefit base (the OASDI taxable maximum) for calendar year 2026 is $184,500.

That is the maximum amount of an individual worker's covered earnings subject to the 6.2% employee and 6.2% employer Social Security (OASDI) payroll tax, and the maximum amount of earnings creditable toward Social Security benefit computations for 2026. There is no comparable cap for Medicare Hospital Insurance (HI); the 1.45%/1.45% HI tax applies to all earnings.

SOURCE BASIS (all Social Security Administration, all agreeing)

1. SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, 'Contribution and Benefit Base' (ssa.gov/OACT/COLA/cbb.html) — year-by-year table: 2025 = $176,100; 2026 = $184,500; 2027 = $192,300.
2. SSA Publication No. 05-10003, 2026 update (ssa.gov/pubs/EN-05-10003.pdf) — 'Social Security taxes 2025 / 2026: Employee/employer (each) 6.2% on earnings up to $176,100 / 6.2% on earnings up to $184,500'; self-employed '12.4% on earnings up to $176,100 / 12.4% on earnings up to $184,500'.
3. SSA Fast Facts & Figures About Social Security, 2026 — 'Maximum earnings subject to Social Security taxes, 2026: OASDI 184,500; HI No limit'.
4. SSA Office of the Chief Actuary, Detailed Calculator update page (ssa.gov/oact/anypia/update.html) — 'Contribution and benefit base for 2026: $184,500'; 'Old-law' contribution and benefit base for 2026: $137,100.

The figure was announced in the fall of 2025 together with the December 2025 COLA (2.8%) and the 2026 wage-indexed amounts, so this is an official, final determination — not a projection. (The SSA site, as fetched, also already carries the 2027 base of $192,300; that is a different year and must not be substituted for the 2026 answer.)

HOW THE FIGURE IS DERIVED (statutory formula, for verification)

Under section 230 of the Social Security Act, the base for any year Y after 1994 equals the 1994 base of $60,600 multiplied by the ratio of the national average wage index (AWI) for year Y-2 to the AWI for 1992, rounded to the nearest multiple of $300, and never reduced below the prior year's base. For 2026 the relevant AWI is the 2024 AWI of $69,846.57 (announced fall 2025):

  $60,600 x ($69,846.57 / $22,935.42) = $184,548.5... , rounded to nearest $300 = $184,500

Check: $184,500 / $300 = 615 exactly (valid rounding result). $184,500 > $176,100 (2025 base), so the no-decrease floor is not binding.

DERIVED TAX AMOUNTS AT THE 2026 BASE (for convenience; not part of the ask)

- Maximum employee OASDI tax: $184,500 x 6.2% = $11,439.00
- Maximum employer OASDI tax per employee: $184,500 x 6.2% = $11,439.00
- Combined employee + employer maximum: $22,878.00
- Maximum self-employed OASDI tax (SECA): $184,500 x 12.4% = $22,878.00
- Medicare (HI): no earnings limit in 2026; the 1.45% employee / 1.45% employer (2.9% self-employed) rates apply to all covered earnings, plus the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax above the statutory thresholds ($200,000 single / $250,000 joint), which are not indexed and are not part of the contribution and benefit base.

SCOPE NOTES / COMMONLY CONFUSED ADJACENT FIGURES (2026)

- 2026 COLA: 2.8% (affects benefits, not the base).
- 2026 old-law contribution and benefit base: $137,100 (used for special-minimum benefits, Railroad Retirement, and ERISA computations — not the payroll-tax cap).
- 2026 earnings test exempt amounts: $24,480 (under FRA, $1-for-$2) and $65,160 (year of FRA, $1-for-$3); no limit at or above FRA.
- 2026 one work credit: $1,890 (max four credits = $7,560).
- 2027 contribution and benefit base: $192,300 (already announced; not the answer to this question).

CAVEATS

- The base is per worker, per year, and applies to wage and self-employment earnings combined: a worker with both W-2 wages and self-employment income applies the cap to the combined total (self-employment earnings are taxable only up to the base minus taxable wages).
- A worker with multiple employers whose combined wages exceed $184,500 is due a refund of excess employee OASDI tax withheld (claimed on the individual return); each employer separately withholds up to the base.
- Figure is in nominal US dollars for tax year 2026; no rounding or conversion is needed.

question: M12
answer:
## Answer

The 2026 limit on an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan, before any catch-up contribution, is **$24,500**.

This is the IRC §402(g)(1) limit on the exclusion for elective deferrals. It is also the limit on the employee's compensation that may be deferred — the statutory cap is the lesser of $24,500 or 100% of the employee's compensation.

## Authority

- IRS Notice 2025-67, *2026 Cost-of-Living Adjusted Limitations* (published in IRB 2025-49, page 761): "The limitation under section 402(g)(1) on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in section 402(g)(3), which includes elective deferrals made to the Thrift Savings Plan, is increased from $23,500 to $24,500."
- IRS, Retirement Topics – 401(k) and Profit-Sharing Plan Contribution Limits: "The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments."
- IRS, Retirement Topics – Contributions: "The basic limit on elective deferrals is $24,500 in 2026, $23,500 in 2025, $23,000 in 2024 and $22,500 in 2023, or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less."
- IRS, COLA Increases for Dollar Limitations (2026 table): Elective deferrals — $24,500 (2026), $23,500 (2025), $23,000 (2024), $22,500 (2023).
- IRS Publication 525 (2026): the overall elective deferral limit is $24,500 for 2026.

## What this figure covers and does not cover

| Item | 2026 amount | Relation to the $24,500 |
|---|---|---|
| §402(g)(1) elective deferral limit (pre-tax **and** designated Roth) | $24,500 | The answer |
| Age 50+ catch-up (§414(v)(2)(B)(i)) | $8,000 | Excluded by the request; sits **on top of** the $24,500 |
| Age 60–63 enhanced catch-up (§414(v)(2)(E)(i)) | $11,250 | Excluded by the request; replaces (not adds to) the $8,000 |
| §415(c) annual additions limit (deferrals + employer money + forfeitures) | $72,000 | Separate outer limit; catch-up contributions do not count against it |
| §401(a)(17) compensation cap used for contributions/matching | $360,000 | Separate limit |
| SIMPLE 401(k) / SIMPLE IRA deferral limit | $17,000 | Sub-limit for SIMPLE plans; still counts toward the $24,500 aggregate |
| 2025 / 2027 elective deferral limit | $23,500 / $25,500 | Adjacent-year context only |

## HR / plan-administration notes that change how the number is applied (not the number itself)

1. **It is a per-employee limit, not a per-plan limit.** An employee who defers to a 401(k) and also to a 403(b), a governmental 457(b), a SARSEP, or a SIMPLE plan must aggregate those deferrals against the single $24,500 ceiling. Payroll should collect a deferral-aggregation attestation at enrollment and at each open enrollment for any employee flagged as having another employer plan.
2. **The plan may impose a lower limit.** The $24,500 is a maximum, not an entitlement. Plan-document caps, per-paycheck percentage caps, and ADP/ACP-corrective limits for highly compensated employees (HCE threshold for 2026 remains $160,000) can all hold an individual below $24,500.
3. **Roth and pre-tax share the same $24,500.** Designated Roth 401(k) contributions are elective deferrals under §402(g); they are not additive. If the plan offers both, the combined total is capped at $24,500.
4. **Excess deferrals must be corrected.** Amounts above $24,500 (excluding valid catch-up) are includible in gross income and are corrected by distribution of the excess plus earnings by April 15 of the following year; if not timely distributed, the excess is taxed twice and can raise plan qualification issues. This is the operational reason the figure matters to HR/payroll, not just to the participant.
5. **The figure is final, not projected.** Notice 2025-67 is the published annual COLA notice; no further 2026 adjustment is expected. Statutory §402(g) amounts round to the nearest $500, which is why the increase lands on $24,500 rather than an odd dollar figure.
6. **Scope.** This is the US federal limit only. It is not a state limit, not a plan-specific limit, and not a total-contribution limit. It does not address IRA limits ($7,500 for 2026), which are a separate bucket with their own rules.

## One-line version for an employee handbook or payroll system

> For 2026, you may defer up to $24,500 of your pay into the 401(k) plan (or 100% of your compensation, if less). If you are 50 or older, you may defer an additional $8,000 — or $11,250 if you turn 60, 61, 62, or 63 in 2026 — if the plan permits catch-up contributions. The $24,500 limit is a personal limit that applies across all employers' elective-deferral plans combined.
