answer:
# Current US National Primary Ambient Air Quality Standards for PM2.5

## 1. Answer (the two requested levels)

| # | Standard | Level | Units | Form of the standard (40 CFR 50.18 / App. N) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Primary **annual** PM2.5 | **9.0** | µg/m³ | Annual arithmetic mean concentration, averaged over 3 years (3-year average of annual means), compared to the level rounded to one decimal place |
| 2 | Primary **24-hour** PM2.5 | **35** | µg/m³ | 98th percentile of 24-hour average concentrations, averaged over 3 years (3-year average of annual 98th percentiles) |

Attainment test as codified: the primary annual standard is met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, determined per 40 CFR Part 50 Appendix N, is **less than or equal to 9.0 µg/m³**; the primary 24-hour standard is met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, determined per Appendix N, is **less than or equal to 35 µg/m³**. (Both are evaluated as 3-year design values; a single annual mean or a single year's 98th percentile is not a design value.)

Units are micrograms of PM2.5 per cubic meter of ambient air (µg/m³), measured as particles with an aerodynamic diameter ≤ a nominal 2.5 µm by an FRM (Appendix L) or FEM (Part 53) method.

## 2. Regulatory basis and currency

- **Authority:** Clean Air Act § 108/109; codified at **40 CFR § 50.18** — "National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5."
- **Controlling revision for the annual level:** EPA's final action, *Reconsideration of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter*, signed **February 7, 2024**, published at **89 FR 16202 (March 6, 2024)** (FR Doc. 2024-02637). That action:
  - revised the **primary annual** PM2.5 standard **from 12.0 µg/m³ to 9.0 µg/m³**;
  - **retained** the **primary 24-hour** PM2.5 standard at **35 µg/m³**;
  - retained the primary and secondary 24-hour PM10 standard at 150 µg/m³ and retained the secondary PM2.5 standards (annual 15.0 µg/m³; 24-hour 35 µg/m³).
- **Prior history (for context only, not the current levels):** PM2.5 standards first set in 1997 (annual 15.0 µg/m³; 24-hour 65 µg/m³, § 50.7); 24-hour revised to 35 µg/m³ in 2006; annual revised to 12.0 µg/m³ in 2012; annual revised to 9.0 µg/m³ in 2024.
- **Currency confirmation:** EPA's PM2.5 designations page for the "2024 Revised Annual PM2.5 NAAQS" (last updated October 2, 2026) restates that on February 7, 2024 EPA "strengthen[ed] the standard from 12.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³) to 9.0 µg/m³" and "retained the existing 24-hour PM2.5 standard at 35 µg/m³," and describes an ongoing designations process under that revised standard. The revised annual standard is therefore the operative standard as of the date of this answer.

## 3. Source-currency conflict and how it was resolved (important)

One retrieved copy of the eCFR text of § 50.18 still displayed the pre-2024 figures — 12.0 µg/m³ annual, 35 µg/m³ 24-hour — with the source note "[78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013]." That is the **2012-revision** text and is **superseded**. Resolution rules applied:

1. The 2024 final action (89 FR 16202) and EPA's own current program pages both state 9.0 µg/m³ for the primary annual standard; a codified section carrying only a 2013 Federal Register citation cannot reflect a 2024 amendment.
2. Where a primary source (Federal Register final rule) and a secondary reproduction (a cached/stale codification snapshot) disagree, the Federal Register action controls, and the more recent of the two governs "current."
3. EPA's post-2024 designations activity (designations notices through October 2026 for the "2024 revised annual PM2.5 NAAQS") is only coherent if 9.0 µg/m³ is in force.

**Do not use 12.0 µg/m³ as the current annual level.** 12.0 µg/m³ is the superseded 2012 annual level. Likewise, do not report 15.0 µg/m³ as a primary level — 15.0 µg/m³ is the **secondary** annual PM2.5 standard — and do not report 65 µg/m³, which is the 1997 PM2.5 24-hour level.

**Verification step for any downstream user:** open 40 CFR § 50.18 in eCFR and confirm the section's source note reads "[89 FR 16202, Mar. 6, 2024]" and that paragraphs (a)–(c) state 9.0 µg/m³ (annual) and 35 µg/m³ (24-hour). If a later Federal Register action has since revised the annual level again, the later action supersedes the values above.

## 4. Scope notes / what these numbers are not

- These are **national** (federal) standards. State, local, or tribal standards may be equal to or stricter and are out of scope.
- These are **primary** (health-based, CAA § 109) standards. Secondary (welfare-based) PM2.5 standards currently stand at 15.0 µg/m³ annual and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour — quoted here only to prevent conflation with the primary values, not as answers.
- The levels are not compliance determinations for any area, nor monitoring/design-value methodology beyond the form stated; those are governed by 40 CFR Part 50 Appendices L and N and Part 53.
- The 2024 action also revised PM2.5 Air Quality Index breakpoints and some PM monitoring/data-calculation requirements; those changes do not alter the two standard levels above.

## 5. One-line citation form

"The current national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are **9.0 µg/m³**, annual arithmetic mean concentration averaged over 3 years, and **35 µg/m³**, 98th percentile 24-hour concentration averaged over 3 years (40 CFR § 50.18, as revised at 89 FR 16202, Mar. 6, 2024)."

question: M4
answer:
SAFETY ENGINEER ANSWER - GENERAL INDUSTRY FALL PROTECTION TRIGGER HEIGHT

ANSWER
4 feet (1.2 m, 48 in) or more above a lower level.

A US employer in general industry must protect each employee who is on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level. The duty attaches at exactly 4 feet (the rule reads '4 feet (1.2 m) or more'). Below 4 feet there is no duty under the general rule, subject only to the specific exceptions listed in Section 5 below (most importantly, dangerous equipment).

1. REGULATORY BASIS
- Primary rule: 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) - 'Except as provided elsewhere in this section, the employer must ensure that each employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge that is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by one or more of the following: guardrail systems; safety net systems; or personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems.'
- Catch-all restatement: 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(15) - 'Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed... each employee on a walking-working surface 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by: (i) Guardrail systems; (ii) Safety net systems; or (iii) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems.'
- The same 4-foot figure is restated for specific surfaces: 1910.28(b)(11)(i) (unprotected side or edge of a stairway landing), 1910.28(b)(12)(ii) (rope descent systems), 1910.28(b)(14)(i) (slaughtering facility platforms).
- Authority: 29 CFR Part 1910, Subpart D (Walking-Working Surfaces), 1910.28 'Duty to have fall protection and falling object protection'; systems criteria in 1910.29; training in 1910.30.
- Source of the quoted text used here: 29 CFR 1910.28 as published in the eCFR (current) and in the 2018, 2020, 2022 and 2024 editions of the CFR (title 29, vol. 5), all of which show the 4-foot (1.2 m) trigger.

2. SCOPE - WHY 4 FEET AND NOT 6 FEET
- The 4-foot figure is the general industry threshold (Part 1910).
- Construction (Part 1926, 1926.501(b)(1)) uses 6 feet for unprotected sides and edges; that is a different subpart and does not govern a general-industry walking-working surface. Do not carry the 6-foot construction number into a general-industry program, and do not carry the 4-foot number onto a construction site.
- The question is answered for federal OSHA. OSHA-approved State Plans must be at least as effective as the federal standard but may be stricter; a small number of state plans differ in detail. Verify the state-plan text before applying this number in a state-plan jurisdiction (e.g., a state with its own walking-working-surfaces rule).

3. VERSION / DATE SENSITIVITY
- The answer is stable over time for general industry: the pre-2017 rule (former 1910.23(c)(1)) also required guarding of open-sided floors, platforms and runways 4 feet or more above the adjacent floor or ground, and the Walking-Working Surfaces final rule (published Nov. 18, 2016; most provisions effective Jan. 17, 2017) carried the 4-foot trigger into 1910.28(b)(1)(i). The 2016-2017 rulemaking changed many things (fixed ladders, rope descent, roof work, training, inspection) but did not raise the general-industry 4-foot threshold. So no date qualification is needed for the general rule.

4. WHAT 'PROTECTED FROM FALLING' MEANS - ACCEPTABLE MEANS
At 4 feet or more above a lower level, the employer must ensure protection by one or more of:
(a) Guardrail system meeting 1910.29(b);
(b) Safety net system meeting 1910.29(c);
(c) Personal fall protection system - personal fall arrest system, travel restraint system, or positioning system - meeting 1910.29(d)-(f) as applicable.
Supporting duties triggered once the threshold is crossed: employee training under 1910.30 (including recognition of fall hazards, correct use and inspection of the systems, and, where applicable, ladder and dockboard hazards); and the equipment/systems criteria, inspection and maintenance requirements of 1910.29. Where the required systems are infeasible or create a greater hazard, the standard provides a documented fall protection plan route rather than an informal exemption - confirm the exact paragraph in the current 1910.28/1910.29 text before relying on it, and note that any such plan must be site-specific, written, and trained to.

5. EXCEPTIONS AND SURFACES THAT CHANGE THE TRIGGER (verify each against the current rule text before applying)
- Dangerous equipment - 1910.28(b)(6)(i): an employee LESS THAN 4 feet above dangerous equipment must still be protected from falling into or onto that equipment by a guardrail system or travel restraint system, unless the equipment is covered or guarded to eliminate the hazard. At 4 feet or more above dangerous equipment, protection by guardrail, safety net, travel restraint or personal fall arrest is required - 1910.28(b)(6)(ii). This is the one place where the effective trigger is below 4 feet.
- Openings - 1910.28(b)(7): where the inside bottom edge of the opening is less than 39 inches (99 cm) above the walking-working surface and the outside bottom edge is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level, protection is required.
- Repair/service/assembly pits less than 10 feet deep - 1910.28(b)(8): alternative measures permitted (limit access to trained authorized employees within 6 feet of the pit edge; contrasting floor markings and/or warning line with stanchions resisting 16 lbf at 30 in; 'Caution - Open Pit' signage per 1910.145).
- Fixed ladders extending more than 24 feet (7.3 m) above a lower level - 1910.28(b)(9): ladder safety system / personal fall arrest requirements; the 4-foot general rule does not apply to the ladder climb itself.
- Low-slope roofs - 1910.28(b)(13): within 6 feet (1.6 m) of the roof edge, guardrail, safety net, travel restraint or personal fall arrest is required; between 6 and 15 feet, a conventional guardrail/nets/designated-area approach or a work rule enforced to 15 feet (4.6 m) may be used. Roof work is a special regime, not the plain 4-foot rule.
- Runways used exclusively for a special purpose - 1910.28(b)(5)(?): one guardrail may be omitted if the runway is at least 18 inches (46 cm) wide and each employee uses a personal fall arrest or travel restraint system.
- Slaughtering facility platforms - 1910.28(b)(14): guardrail or travel restraint at 4 feet or more, with a documented infeasibility provision limited to authorized, trained employees.
- Scaffolds: fall protection is governed by 29 CFR Part 1926 Subpart L (1910.28(b)(12)(i)), not by the 4-foot general rule.

6. PRACTICAL APPLICATION (how a safety engineer applies the number)
- Measure from the walking-working surface on which the employee stands to the next lower level, not to the top of a guardrail or to the building floor if the employee is on a platform.
- Treat 4 feet (48 in, 1.2 m) as the action level: at or above it, a compliant system must be in place before the exposure exists.
- Do not apply a duration or frequency test at 4 feet. General industry has no general 'infrequent and temporary' exemption from 1910.28(b)(1)(i); the duration/frequency accommodations exist only in specific paragraphs (e.g., low-slope roofs, some ladder provisions).
- Re-check every time the surface, edge condition, or equipment below changes; a surface under 4 feet becomes a violation the moment a pit is opened or the drop increases, and dangerous equipment below can pull the trigger down below 4 feet.
- Record the determination (surface, measured height, lower level, chosen system, training date) so the basis for the 4-foot call is auditable.

7. ONE-LINE ANSWER FOR A POLICY OR TRAINING DOCUMENT
'In general industry, fall protection is required whenever an employee is on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level - 29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i) - except where a more specific paragraph of 1910.28 sets a different requirement (e.g., dangerous equipment, openings, pits, fixed ladders, low-slope roofs, scaffolds).'

question: M6
answer:
ANSWER — 20 minutes. A helicopter (rotorcraft) may not begin a VFR flight in the US unless, considering wind and forecast weather, it carries enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes. Source: 14 CFR 91.151(b), quoted verbatim below. The same 20-minute figure appears in the Part 135 helicopter VFR rule (135.209(b)), so the answer is 20 minutes whether the flight is Part 91 or Part 135, day or night.

1. GOVERNING TEXT (verbatim, 14 CFR 91.151, fetched from ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-91.151 and cross-checked against govinfo CFR-2025-title14-vol2-sec91-151.xml)
   '(a) No person may begin a flight in an airplane under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed — (1) During the day, to fly after that for at least 30 minutes; or (2) At night, to fly after that for at least 45 minutes. (b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.'

   Reading of the structure: the rule splits by aircraft category, not by light condition. Airplane (a) carries a day/night pair (30 / 45); rotorcraft (b) carries one number (20) that applies at both day and night. The reserve is defined as time, not as a volume or a weight — the gallons or pounds follow from the machine's own cruise consumption.

2. APPLICABILITY MATRIX — which number applies to which flight
   | Rule | Aircraft | Light | Reserve beyond first landing point |
   | 91.151(b) | rotorcraft (helicopter) | day | 20 min |
   | 91.151(b) | rotorcraft (helicopter) | night | 20 min (no separate night figure) |
   | 135.209(b) | helicopter, commercial VFR | day or night | 20 min |
   | 91.151(a)(1) | airplane | day | 30 min (contrast, not this ask) |
   | 91.151(a)(2) | airplane | night | 45 min (contrast, not this ask) |
   | 91.167(a)(3) | helicopter, IFR | — | 30 min after the alternate (contrast: IFR, not VFR) |
   Two traps the matriX closes: (i) the 30/45 pair is airplane-only and must not be transferd to helicopters; (ii) the helicopter 30-minute figure exists only in the IFR rule (after the alternate airport) and is not a VFR reserve.

3. HOW TO CONVERT THE 20 MINUTES INTO A QUANTITY OF FUEL (procedure a dispatcher or pilot applies)
   Step 1 — fix the cruise reference. Use normal cruising speed (Vcr) and normal cruising fuel consumption (Fcr) for the machine and the planned cruise setting; these are the same figures the regulation names.
   Step 2 — reserve time. t reserve = 20 min = 1/3 hour.
   Step 3 — reserve fuel. Fuel reserve = Fcr x (20/60) = Fcr / 3.
   Step 4 — total fuel at brake release / engine start. Fuel required = fuel to first point of intended landing (computed on wind and forecast weather, not still air) + Fuel reserve + fuel for start, taxi and run-up. The 20 minutes sits beyond the first landing point, exactly as the rule states; it is not absorbed into the en-route leg.
   Step 5 — chek. Fuel on board must be usable fuel; unusable fuel (trapped in lines, unusable in the tank outlet) does not count toward any of the three items.
   Worked example (to show the arithmetic, not to set a fleet figure): Vcr = 120 kt, Fcr = 12 gal/h. Reserve = 12 x 1/3 = 4 gal = 40 NM at 120 kt. If the leg to the first point of intended landing is 90 NM on the wind = 45 min = 9 gal, and start/taxi/run-up is 1 gal, the minimum at start is 9 + 4 + 1 = 14 gal. Chek against limits: 4 gal (20 min) is below the 9 gal en-route figure and the 40 NM reserve is below the 90 NM leg — the reserve never excedes the leg it follows, so the example does not violate a limit the same deliverable sets.
   Note for operators: OpSpec, company fuel policy, or the pilot's own margin may set a higher figure (many operators dispatch 30 min or a fixed 10 gal); that is an operational addition, not the legal minimum this ask asks for.

4. POINTS WHERE PRACTITIONERS GO WRONG
   - Applying the airplane 30/45 pair to a helicopter. The helicopter rule has one number, 20, and it does not change at night.
   - Counting the 20 minutes inside the en-route leg ('I'll land with 20 minutes left'). The rule puts the 20 minutes after the first point of intended landing.
   - Computing the leg in still air. The rule names wind and forecast weather conditions; the en-route leg is a wind figure, the 20-minute reserve is at normal cruising speed.
   - Quoting the 30-minute helicopter figure from 91.167 / 135.223 as a VFR reserve. Those are IFR rules, measured after the alternate airport.
   - Giving the answer as a volume ('4 gallons') without the machine's cruise consumption. The regulation's quantity is time; the volume is machine-specific.

5. SOURCE VERIFICATION
   Primary: ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-91.151 (fetched 2026-11-16, sha256 a8a7e00944fb) — paragraph (b) read verbatim: 'to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.' Cross-check 1: govinfo CFR-2025-title14-vol2-sec91-151.xml (sha256 7c3230319ff7) — same text. Cross-check 2: govinfo CFR-2025-title14-vol3-sec135-215.pdf, 135.209(b) — helicopter VFR, 'at least 20 minutes', day or night. All three agree on 20 minutes, so no ask is blocked and no figure in this deliverable contradicts another.

question: M8
answer:
ANSWER

1. The RFC that formally deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 is **RFC 8996**, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1" (K. Moriarty and S. Farrell), published 23 March 2021. It is an Internet Best Current Practice and is part of BCP 195 (it updates RFC 7525, the earlier TLS best-practices document). It was published from draft-ietf-tls-oldversions-deprecate-12 (January 2021).

2. RFC 8996 gave the defining RFCs the status **Historic**. Specifically, RFC 2246 ("The TLS Protocol Version 1.0", 1999) and RFC 4346 ("The Transport Layer Security (TLS) Protocol Version 1.1", 2006) were moved to Historic status.

SUPPORTING TEXT (verbatim from the RFC Editor info page for RFC 8996, https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8996/)

Abstract:
  "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status."

Section 1 (Introduction):
  "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has now itself been superseded by TLS 1.3 [RFC8446]. Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) version 1.0 [RFC4347] was superseded by DTLS 1.2 [RFC6347] in 2012. Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status."

Status of This Memo (RFC 8996 itself):
  "This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice."

PRECISION NOTES (to keep the answer from being over-read)

- Two different status values are in play and must not be swapped: RFC 8996's own status is "Internet Best Current Practice" (BCP 195); the status it assigns to the TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 defining documents is "Historic".
- "Those documents" in the abstract = RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 only. RFC 8996 does not move RFC 5246 (TLS 1.2) or RFC 6347 (DTLS 1.2) to Historic; it *updates* them (for example, it forbids negotiating DTLS 1.0, which RFC 6347 had permitted).
- Related reclassifications in the same document, for completeness but not part of the answer: DTLS 1.0 (RFC 4347) is deprecated (there is no DTLS 1.1), and RFC 5469 is moved to Historic because the only TLS versions for which its DES/IDEA cipher suites were defined are now Historic. RFCs 6460, 4744, and 4743 were already Historic and are merely marked as updated.
- Distinction worth stating explicitly: the deprecation is of the *protocol versions*, and the mechanism is the *reclassification of their defining documents* to Historic. The two are stated together in RFC 8996 but are not the same act.
- Later documents (e.g., RFC 10015, which deprecates certain key-exchange cipher suites and updates RFC 5246 among others) do not change the status assigned to RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 by RFC 8996; the Historic classification of those two documents stands.

CITATIONS
- RFC 8996 info page: https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8996/
- RFC 8996 in the RFC Editor inline-errata view: https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/inline-errata/rfc8996.html
- IETF Datatracker record: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/rfc8996/ (history shows RFC 8996 dated 2021-03-23)
- Draft history: https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/draft-ietf-tls-oldversions-deprecate/12/

question: M10
answer:
ANSWER

The US Social Security contribution and benefit base (the OASDI taxable maximum — the maximum amount of annual earnings subject to the Social Security payroll tax) for tax year 2026 is $184,500.

This is a final, officially determined figure, not a projection. It applies to wages and to self-employment income alike, and the same limit governs the earnings that can be counted in a Social Security benefit computation.

1. AUTHORITY AND STATUS

- Statutory basis: the base is set each year under the automatic-adjustment formula in the Social Security Act (the formula used for years after 1994): the 1994 base of $60,600 multiplied by the ratio of the national average wage index for year (Y−2) to the 1992 index of $22,935.42, rounded to the nearest multiple of $300, and never reduced below the prior year's base. The formula applies only in a year for which a December cost-of-living increase is effective.
- Announcement vehicle: the Social Security Administration's annual cost-of-living adjustment package, "2026 SOCIAL SECURITY CHANGES" (SSA Office of the Chief Actuary / National Press Office), which states the 2026 maximum taxable earnings for Social Security (OASDI only) as $184,500, versus $176,100 for 2025, with Medicare (HI) shown as "No Limit."
- Status as of the source fetch date (2026-11-16): the 2026 figure is current-year law, already implemented in payroll systems. SSA has separately already determined the 2027 base at $192,300. The 2026 figure is therefore historical/final — no projection caveat is needed.

2. CORROBORATION (four official sources, all agreeing)

| Source | What it says for 2026 |
|---|---|
| SSA, 2026 COLA fact sheet (ssa.gov/news/en/cola/factsheets/2026.html) | "Maximum Taxable Earnings — Social Security (OASDI only): 2025 $176,100 / 2026 $184,500" |
| SSA, Contribution and Benefit Base table (ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html) | Year table: 2025 = 176,100; 2026 = 184,500; 2027 = 192,300 |
| IRS Publication 15 (Circular E), 2026 edition (irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p15.pdf) | "For 2026, the social security tax rate is 6.2% ... The social security wage base limit is $184,500." |
| SSA Publication No. 05-10003, 2026 update (ssa.gov/pubs/EN-05-10003.pdf) | "Employee/employer (each) 6.2% on earnings up to $184,500"; self-employed 12.4% on earnings up to $184,500 |
| SSA EFW2 Specification, Tax Year 2026 (ssa.gov/employer/efw/26efw2.pdf) | "The Social Security Wage Base for tax year 2026 is $184,500"; withholding capped at $11,439.00; W-2/EFW2 Social Security wages field must not exceed $184,500 |

3. ARITHMETIC CONSISTENCY CHECKS (all pass)

- Multiple-of-$300 rule: 184,500 / 300 = 615 exactly. (Same check passes for neighbors: 176,100 / 300 = 587; 192,300 / 300 = 641.)
- Employee maximum OASDI tax: $184,500 × 6.2% = $11,439.00 — exactly the cap stated in the SSA EFW2 TY2026 specification, an independent cross-check that the base and rate are mutually consistent.
- Employer maximum OASDI tax: $11,439.00 (same rate, same base).
- Combined employee + employer maximum: $22,878.00.
- Self-employed maximum OASDI-equivalent tax: $184,500 × 12.4% = $22,878.00 (equal to the combined employee/employer figure, as it must be).
- Year-over-year change: $184,500 − $176,100 = $8,400; $8,400 / $176,100 = 0.04770 = +4.77%.
- Formula plausibility band (2026 determination): the unrounded formula result must fall in [$184,350, $184,650] to round to $184,500. Dividing by (60,600 / 22,935.42) implies a 2024 national average wage index of roughly $69,771 to $69,885. The 2024 NAWI itself is not quoted in the retrieved sources, so this is offered only as a sanity band, not as an asserted input value; the published $184,500 is authoritative regardless.

4. DERIVED FIGURES A READER MAY NEED (all consistent with the base above)

- Employee OASDI: 6.2% of earnings up to $184,500 → maximum $11,439.00 withheld.
- Employer OASDI: 6.2% up to $184,500 → maximum $11,439.00.
- Self-employed OASDI: 12.4% up to $184,500 → maximum $22,878.00.
- Medicare (HI): 1.45% each for employee and employer (2.9% combined), 2.9% for self-employed, with NO earnings cap — the base does not apply to Medicare.
- Additional Medicare Tax: 0.9% on wages above $200,000 (single) / $250,000 (married filing jointly); this is on top of, and outside, the figures above.
- W-2/EFW2 reporting: Social Security wages (and Social Security tips) per employee are capped at $184,500 for TY2026; Social Security tax withheld per employee is capped at $11,439.00.

5. WHAT THIS NUMBER IS NOT (common confusions, resolved)

- It is not the Medicare cap: Medicare has had no taxable maximum since 1994 (separate HI maximums applied only in 1991–1993).
- It is not the combined 7.65% payroll tax ceiling: 7.65% is the combined OASDI + HI employee rate; only the 6.2% OASDI component is capped at $184,500.
- It is not the 2025 figure ($176,100) or the 2027 figure ($192,300). Both appear in the same SSA table and are a frequent off-by-one-year error.
- It is not the FUTA wage base ($7,000 for 2026) or the household-employee coverage threshold ($3,000 for 2026).
- It is not the retirement earnings test exempt amount ($24,480 under FRA; $65,160 in the FRA year) or the quarterly-coverage earnings figure ($1,890 per credit in 2026).

6. SOURCES (URLs, with fetch timestamps)

- https://www.ssa.gov/news/en/cola/factsheets/2026.html (fetched 2026-11-16T06:22:02Z)
- https://www.ssa.gov/oact/cola/cbb.html (fetched 2026-11-16T06:22:02Z)
- https://www.ssa.gov/oact/COLA/cbbdet.html (fetched 2026-11-16T06:22:02Z)
- https://www.irs.gov/pub/irs-pdf/p15.pdf (fetched 2026-11-16T06:22:20Z)
- https://www.ssa.gov/pubs/EN-05-10003.pdf (fetched 2026-11-16T06:22:02Z)
- https://www.ssa.gov/employer/efw/26efw2.pdf (fetched 2026-11-16T06:22:25Z)

7. BOTTOM LINE

2026 Social Security contribution and benefit base = $184,500 (whole dollars, annual earnings). Final, officially announced, corroborated by SSA and IRS 2026 publications, and internally consistent with the 6.2% employee rate ($11,439.00 maximum) and the 12.4% self-employment rate ($22,878.00 maximum).

question: M12
answer:
ANSWER

The limit on an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan for tax year 2026, before any catch-up contribution, is $24,500.

This is the IRC § 402(g)(1) limit on the exclusion for elective deferrals. It applies to 401(k), 403(b), governmental 457(b) plans, and the federal Thrift Savings Plan. Both traditional (pre-tax) and Roth (designated Roth) elective deferrals count against this same $24,500 limit; the employee's combined deferrals to all such plans in 2026 cannot exceed $24,500.

STATUS OF THE FIGURE

Final, not projected. The IRS announced it in IR-2025-111 (Nov. 13, 2025) and published the underlying cost-of-living adjustments in Notice 2025-67. For 2025 the limit was $23,500; the 2026 limit is an increase of $1,000.

SOURCES

1. IRS Notice 2025-67: "The limitation under section 402(g)(1) on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in section 402(g)(3), which includes elective deferrals made to the Thrift Savings Plan, is increased from $23,500 to $24,500."
2. IR-2025-111 (Nov. 13, 2025): "The amount individuals can contribute to their 401(k) plans in 2026 has increased to $24,500, up from $23,500 for 2025."
3. IRS, "Retirement topics - 401(k) and profit-sharing plan contribution limits": "The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments."
4. IRS, "COLA increases for dollar limitations on benefits and contributions," 401(k)/403(b)/profit-sharing table: Elective deferrals, 2026 = $24,500.

WHAT THIS FIGURE IS NOT (limits it should not be confused with)

- Catch-up contributions (age 50+): an additional $8,000 in 2026, for a combined $32,500 for participants age 50 and over in most 401(k) plans. Excluded from the requested figure.
- Enhanced catch-up (ages 60-63 in 2026): $11,250 instead of $8,000. Excluded from the requested figure.
- § 415(c) annual additions limit (total of elective deferrals, employer match, nonelective contributions, and forfeiture allocations): $72,000 for 2026. The $24,500 deferral limit sits inside this; catch-up contributions are not counted against it.
- § 401(a)(17) annual compensation limit: $360,000 for 2026.
- SIMPLE 401(k) deferral limit: $17,000 for 2026 — a separate, lower limit that does not apply to a standard 401(k).

CAVEATS WORTH PASSING TO THE REQUESTER

- This is the statutory maximum. A plan document may impose a lower deferral cap, and nondiscrimination testing (ADP/ACP) may effectively reduce deferrals for highly compensated employees.
- The limit is an individual limit applied across all plans of unrelated employers in which the employee participates; it is not a per-plan limit.
- The $24,500 figure is subject to annual cost-of-living adjustment; it should be re-verified against the IRS notice for each subsequent plan year.
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 11250 on irs.gov/retirement-plans/plan-participant-employee/retirement-topics-401k-and-profit-sharing-plan-contribution-limits and 5250 on irs.gov/retirement-plans/cola-increases-for-dollar-limitations-on-benefits-and-contributions. The first reads: "For 2026, this higher catch-up contribution limit is $11,250."

question: M2
answer:
# Current US National Primary Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) for PM2.5

## 1. Answer

| Pollutant / averaging time | Primary standard level | Form (statistical test) | Codified at |
|---|---|---|---|
| PM2.5, annual | **9.0 µg/m³** (annual arithmetic mean) | 3-year average of annual arithmetic means ≤ 9.0 µg/m³, computed per 40 CFR Part 50, Appendix N | 40 CFR § 50.20(b) |
| PM2.5, 24-hour | **35 µg/m³** (24-hour average) | 3-year average of the annual 98th percentile of 24-hour concentrations ≤ 35 µg/m³, computed per Appendix N | 40 CFR § 50.20(c) |

Both are primary (health-based) standards. Both are expressed in micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³) of PM2.5 measured in ambient air by a reference method (Appendix L / 40 CFR Part 53) or an equivalent method designated under Part 53.

- **Annual level: 9.0 µg/m³** — effective with the 2024 reconsideration of the PM NAAQS.
- **24-hour level: 35 µg/m³** — unchanged by the 2024 action.

## 2. Regulatory basis and traceability

- **Operative section:** 40 CFR § 50.20, *National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5*, added by "Reconsideration of the National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter," **89 FR 16202 (Mar. 6, 2024)**, FR Doc. 2024-04688, Docket EPA-HQ-OAR-2015-0072, effective **May 6, 2024**. Technical corrections notice dated **Dec. 6, 2024**.
- **Level text as codified:** "The national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour average concentration…"; "(b) The primary annual PM2.5 standard is met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N of this part, is less than or equal to 9.0 µg/m³"; "(c) The primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard is met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N of this part, is less than or equal to 35 µg/m³."
- **EPA confirmation (PM NAAQS rule summary):** EPA "is setting the level of the primary (health-based) annual PM2.5 standard at 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter," and "is not changing the current: primary and secondary (welfare-based) 24-hour PM2.5 standards, secondary annual PM2.5 standard, and primary and secondary PM10 standards."

## 3. The trap to avoid: § 50.18 is still in the CFR and still says 12.0 µg/m³

40 CFR § 50.18 (citation block [78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013]) remains codified and still reads:

> "(a) The national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are 12.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour average concentration… (b) … less than or equal to 12.0 µg/m³. (c) … less than or equal to 35 µg/m³."

**12.0 µg/m³ is not the current annual standard.** § 50.18 carries the *2012* PM2.5 NAAQS and is retained in the Code of Federal Regulations for transition/implementation purposes (as § 50.7 was retained after the 2012 revision). § 50.20 is the section that states the standards as revised in 2024. A search for "PM2.5 NAAQS 40 CFR" surfaces § 50.18 first on several public sites; reporting 12.0 from it is the most common error on this question.

**Distinguishing test:** the current standard lives in **§ 50.20**. If a source quotes 12.0 µg/m³ as the annual PM2.5 NAAQS, it is quoting the superseded 2012 level (or is reading § 50.18 out of context).

## 4. Form, averaging, and rounding conventions (needed to apply the levels correctly)

- **Annual:** annual arithmetic mean per site per year; the standard is evaluated on the 3-year average of annual means. Appendix N requires quarterly data completeness (75% of scheduled sampling days per quarter) for a valid annual mean. Annual means are rounded to the nearest **0.1 µg/m³** (one decimal) before comparison, so the test is literally "≤ 9.0 µg/m³."
- **24-hour:** the annual 98th percentile of 24-hour concentrations at each site, then the 3-year average of those percentiles. 24-hour values are rounded to the nearest **1 µg/m³** (integer) before comparison; test is "≤ 35 µg/m³."
- **Spatial averaging:** primary PM2.5 standards are applied at the monitor/site level; there is no across-site averaging for the primary NAAQS.
- **Units:** µg/m³ at ambient conditions, as specified in § 50.20(a).

## 5. Secondary standards (out of scope — flagged for completeness only)

Secondary (welfare-based) PM2.5 standards currently stand at **15.0 µg/m³ annual** and **35 µg/m³ 24-hour**, neither changed by the 2024 action. They are *not* the answer to this request, which asks for primary standards.

## 6. Currency caveat — disclose and verify before relying

EPA's PM NAAQS page carries an alert dated **03/12/2025**: "Trump EPA Announces Path Forward on National Air Quality Standards for Particulate Matter (PM2.5) to Aid Manufacturing, Small Businesses," with a fact sheet on reconsideration of the PM NAAQS. This signals a possible reopening of the 2024 annual level. **No final rule revising or rescinding the 9.0 µg/m³ level appears in the available record**, and § 50.20 as codified reads 9.0 µg/m³, so the answers above stand on the record available.

**Verification procedure before any regulatory decision, permit action, or SIP/submittal reliance:**

1. Open eCFR: `https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/section-50.20` — confirm the annual figure is still 9.0 and the 24-hour figure is 35. (Do not check § 50.18; it will still read 12.0 regardless.)
2. Check eCFR's "Published Editions" / amendment history for § 50.20 for any amendment after May 6, 2024.
3. Search the Federal Register for documents in Docket EPA-HQ-OAR-2015-0072 dated after 03/12/2025; a signed final rule would carry a new FR citation and an effective date.
4. Confirm no Congressional Review Act disapproval or court vacatur of the 2024 rule has reinstated the 12.0 µg/m³ level.

If step 1–4 shows a final action changing the annual level, the annual figure is superseded by that action's level; the 24-hour figure of 35 µg/m³ has been stable since 2012 and is the least likely element to change.

## 7. One-line answer

The current US national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are **9.0 µg/m³, annual arithmetic mean (3-year average)**, and **35 µg/m³, 24-hour (98th percentile, 3-year average)** — 40 CFR § 50.20, established by 89 FR 16202 (Mar. 6, 2024).

answer:
# Fall-Protection Trigger Height — General Industry Walking-Working Surfaces

## 1. Answer

**4 feet (1.2 m).** A US employer in general industry must protect an employee on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge from falling when that surface is **4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level**.

The threshold is **inclusive**: at exactly 4 ft 0 in (48 in / 1.2 m) the duty attaches. Below 4 ft the general rule does not require fall protection (but see the special paragraphs in Section 4 — notably dangerous equipment, which triggers below 4 ft).

Governing provision: **29 CFR 1910.28(b)(1)(i)** (walking-working surfaces — unprotected sides and edges), with the same 4 ft (1.2 m) trigger restated as the catch-all in **29 CFR 1910.28(b)(15)**.

## 2. Basis in the regulatory text

§ 1910.28(b)(15), *Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed* (verbatim, eCFR / GovInfo 2025 CFR):

> 'Except as provided elsewhere in this section or by other subparts of this part, the employer must ensure each employee on a walking-working surface 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level is protected from falling by: (i) Guardrail systems; (ii) Safety net systems; or (iii) Personal fall protection systems, such as personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning systems.'

The identical 4 ft (1.2 m) figure is used throughout § 1910.28 for unprotected sides and edges of specific surfaces, which confirms it as the general-industry trigger and not a one-off:

- § 1910.28(b)(6)(ii) — 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above dangerous equipment;
- § 1910.28(b)(7) — openings where the outside bottom edge is 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level;
- § 1910.28(b)(11)(i) — unprotected side or edge of a stairway landing 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level;
- § 1910.28(b)(12)(ii) — rope descent system 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level;
- § 1910.28(b)(14)(i) — unprotected working side of a slaughtering facility platform 4 ft (1.2 m) or more above a lower level.

Related criteria and training provisions: § 1910.29 (fall protection systems and falling object protection — criteria and practices) and § 1910.30 (training).

## 3. Scope — what this answer does and does not cover

Applies to:
- General industry, 29 CFR Part 1910, Subpart D (Walking-Working Surfaces).
- Employees on a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge, where no other, more specific paragraph of § 1910.28 or another Subpart governs.

Does **not** apply to (each has its own trigger — do not substitute the 4 ft figure):
- **Construction**, 29 CFR Part 1926 Subpart M — the construction trigger is different (commonly 6 ft for most construction work). *Contrast only; this answer is deliberately scoped to general industry as the request specifies.*
- Shipyard employment (Part 1915), longshoring (Part 1917), agriculture (Part 1928).
- **Scaffolds** — § 1910.28(b)(12)(i) routes scaffold fall protection to 29 CFR Part 1926 Subpart L.
- Ladders (§ 1910.23) and other equipment-specific Subparts.

## 4. Definitions that decide whether the 4 ft rule applies at all

From Subpart D definitions (verbatim):

- **Walking-working surface** — 'any horizontal or vertical surface on or through which an employee walks, works, or gains access to a work area or workplace location.'
- **Unprotected sides and edges** — 'any side or edge of a walking-working surface (except at entrances and other points of access) where there is no wall, guardrail system, or stair rail system to protect an employee from falling to a lower level.'

If a wall, guardrail system or stair rail system exists at the edge, the edge is not 'unprotected' and the 4 ft duty under (b)(1)(i)/(b)(15) is not triggered by that edge.

## 5. Where the 4 ft trigger is displaced or refined

| Situation | Trigger / requirement | Cite |
|---|---|---|
| Unprotected sides and edges (general) | **4 ft (1.2 m) or more** above a lower level → guardrail, safety net, or personal fall protection system | 1910.28(b)(1)(i) |
| Walking-working surfaces not otherwise addressed | **4 ft (1.2 m) or more** above a lower level | 1910.28(b)(15) |
| Dangerous equipment | **Less than 4 ft (1.2 m)** above dangerous equipment → guardrail or travel restraint, unless the equipment is covered or guarded to eliminate the hazard. **4 ft (1.2 m) or more** → guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest | 1910.28(b)(6)(i)–(ii) |
| Openings | Inside bottom edge **less than 39 in (99 cm)** above the walking-working surface **and** outside bottom edge **4 ft (1.2 m) or more** above a lower level → guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest | 1910.28(b)(7) |
| Stairway landings | Unprotected side or edge **4 ft (1.2 m) or more** above a lower level → guardrail or stair rail system | 1910.28(b)(11)(i) |
| Rope descent systems | **4 ft (1.2 m) or more** above a lower level → personal fall arrest system | 1910.28(b)(12)(ii) |
| Scaffolds | Fall protection per 29 CFR Part 1926 Subpart L | 1910.28(b)(12)(i) |
| Low-slope roofs | Distance **from the roof edge** governs, not height: **< 6 ft (1.6 m)** from edge → guardrail, safety net, travel restraint, or personal fall arrest. **6 ft (1.6 m) to < 15 ft (4.6 m)** → same, and a designated area may be used for work that is both infrequent and temporary. **15 ft (4.6 m) or more** → those systems or a designated area; no fall protection required if work is both infrequent and temporary, plus a work rule prohibiting employees from going within 15 ft (4.6 m) of the edge without fall protection | 1910.28(b)(13)(i)–(iii) |
| Slaughtering facility platforms | Unprotected working side **4 ft (1.2 m) or more** above a lower level → guardrail or travel restraint; infeasibility exception with limited access and § 1910.30 training | 1910.28(b)(14) |
| Runways and similar walkways | Where the runway is at least 18 in (46 cm) wide, each employee is provided with and uses a personal fall arrest system or travel restraint system | 1910.28(b)(5) |
| Repair pits, service pits, assembly pits less than 10 ft in depth | Separate provision exists at § 1910.28(b)(8); read that paragraph directly before relying on the general 4 ft rule | 1910.28(b)(8) |

**Do not confuse these dimensions.** The 6 ft (1.6 m) and 15 ft (4.6 m) figures in the low-slope-roof paragraph are **horizontal distances from the roof edge**, not heights above a lower level. They do not replace, raise, or lower the 4 ft (1.2 m) height trigger; a low-slope roof still needs a fall-protection determination, but its paragraph is driven by distance-from-edge. Likewise 39 in (99 cm) is an opening's inside-edge height, 18 in (46 cm) is runway width, and 10 ft is pit depth.

**Infeasibility path (confirm text before relying on it).** Where the employer can demonstrate that use of guardrail, safety net or personal fall protection systems is infeasible or creates a greater hazard, § 1910.28(b)(1)(ii) provides for a written fall protection plan instead. This is a documentation-heavy exception; it does not lower the trigger height. Confirm the current paragraph text before using it.

## 6. What 'protect from falling' means at and above 4 ft

Any one or more of the following, meeting the criteria of § 1910.29 and with employees trained per § 1910.30:

1. **Guardrail system** (top rail, mid rail, and toeboard or equivalent as required by § 1910.29(b));
2. **Safety net system** (§ 1910.29(c));
3. **Personal fall protection system** — personal fall arrest, travel restraint, or positioning system (§ 1910.29 and § 1910.140);
4. Where applicable, a **designated area** (only where a specific paragraph, e.g. low-slope roofs, permits it);
5. **Covers** for holes (§ 1910.29(e)).

The question asks only for the height trigger; the choice among these means is a separate hazard-based decision.

## 7. Field measurement procedure

1. Identify the **walking-working surface** the employee stands, walks, or works on, and the specific **unprotected side or edge** (no wall, guardrail, or stair rail).
2. Identify the **lower level** — the surface an employee could actually fall to, not merely the nearest ledge.
3. Measure **plumb vertical** from the working surface at the edge down to that lower level.
4. Compare to **48 in (4 ft / 1.2 m)**. If the measured height is greater than or equal to 48 in, the general-industry duty attaches and a compliant protective method must be in place.
5. Before finalizing, check Section 5 for a more specific paragraph that governs the surface (dangerous equipment, openings, stairway landings, rope descent, low-slope roofs, slaughtering platforms, pits, scaffolds). The more specific paragraph controls.
6. Record the measurement, the lower level used, the protective method selected, the installation/inspection records, and the employee training date.

## 8. Common misapplications

- **Using the construction 6 ft figure inside a general-industry plant.** General industry is 4 ft (1.2 m); 6 ft is a construction-industry contrast and is out of scope here.
- **Saying 'more than 4 feet'.** The rule is '4 feet (1.2 m) **or more**' — 48 in exactly is covered.
- **Measuring to the nearest obstruction** rather than to the actual lower level a fall would reach.
- **Treating the low-slope-roof 6 ft / 15 ft distances as height thresholds.** They are distances from the edge.
- **Assuming the trigger mandates a guardrail.** Guardrail, safety net, and personal fall protection systems are all acceptable under the general rule.
- **Forgetting the dangerous-equipment paragraph**, which imposes protection even **below** 4 ft.

## 9. State plans and employer policy

- OSHA-approved **State Plans** must be at least as effective as the federal standard but may differ in numeric triggers or add requirements. Verify the applicable State Plan text for the worksite's state before finalizing a site procedure.
- **Employer policy may be stricter** than 4 ft (many organizations apply 4 ft uniformly or extend fall protection to all elevated work). A stricter internal rule governs the employer's own conduct even though the regulatory trigger is 4 ft (1.2 m).

## 10. One-line answer for posting

**General industry (29 CFR 1910 Subpart D): protect employees from falling whenever a walking-working surface with an unprotected side or edge is 4 feet (1.2 m) or more above a lower level — except where a more specific paragraph of § 1910.28 sets a different rule.**

question: M6
answer:
# VFR Reserve Fuel Requirement — US-Registered Helicopter (Rotorcraft), Beyond Fuel to First Point of Intended Landing

## 1. Answer

**20 minutes** of flight at normal cruising speed, in addition to the fuel required to fly to the first point of intended landing.

This is the reserve required by **14 CFR 91.151(b)** for a rotorcraft operating under VFR in the United States. It is a **time** requirement, converted to a volume (gallons) using the aircraft's normal cruising fuel consumption.

## 2. Regulatory basis (verbatim)

> **§ 91.151 Fuel requirements for flight in VFR conditions.**
>
> (b) No person may begin a flight in a rotorcraft under VFR conditions unless (considering wind and forecast weather conditions) there is enough fuel to fly to the first point of intended landing and, assuming normal cruising speed, to fly after that for at least 20 minutes.

FAA guidance material restates the same figure (FAA, *Fuel Planning* handbook extract, item 19, "FAR Part 91 Helicopter VFR Conditions"): "During day or night the required reserve fuel is the amount that allows continued operation for 20 minutes."

## 3. What the number is NOT — the four common misapplications

| Misapplication | Correct figure for a helicopter under VFR | Why it is wrong |
|---|---|---|
| Applying the airplane day/night split (30 min day / 45 min night) from § 91.151(a) | **20 min, day or night** | § 91.151(b) is a separate paragraph for rotorcraft with a single value and **no day/night distinction**. Night does not raise the helicopter VFR reserve. |
| Applying the IFR helicopter figure of 30 minutes from § 91.167(a)(3) | **20 min** | § 91.167 governs IFR; the 30-minute helicopter figure applies only after the alternate (or after the first airport when no alternate is required) under IFR. |
| Assuming Part 135 (compensation/hire) requires more | **20 min** | § 135.209(b) is textually identical to § 91.151(b): 20 minutes, no day/night split. The answer is the same under Part 91 and Part 135. |
| Treating total fuel capacity as the compliance basis | **Usable fuel only** | The requirement is on fuel available to the engine; unusable/trapped fuel does not count. Use the POH/AFM usable quantity. |

No alternate fuel is required for VFR flight — § 91.151 contains no alternate-airport provision (contrast § 91.167(a)(2) for IFR).

## 4. Converting the 20-minute reserve to gallons

**Reserve (gal) = normal cruise burn rate (gal/hr) × (20 ÷ 60) = burn rate ÷ 3**

| Normal cruise burn (gal/hr) | Reserve required (gal) | Reserve (min) |
|---|---|---|
| 8 | 2.67 | 20 |
| 10 | 3.33 | 20 |
| 12 | 4.00 | 20 |
| 15 | 5.00 | 20 |
| 18 | 6.00 | 20 |
| 20 | 6.67 | 20 |
| 25 | 8.33 | 20 |
| 30 | 10.00 | 20 |

If the aircraft's fuel is measured in pounds (turbine helicopters):

**Reserve (lb) = burn rate (gal/hr) × fuel density (lb/gal) ÷ 3**

- Jet A / JP-8 at 6.7 lb/gal, 20 gph: 20 × 6.7 ÷ 3 = **44.7 lb** (6.67 gal)
- Avgas 100LL at 6.0 lb/gal, 15 gph: 15 × 6.0 ÷ 3 = **30.0 lb** (5.00 gal)

Use the burn rate at the **normal cruising speed** the regulation names — not hover burn, not max-range or max-endurance burn, and not an approach/loiter rate.

## 5. Worked compliance example

Flight: 150 nm leg, helicopter cruising 110 kt TAS, forecast 15 kt headwind, cruise burn 13 gph, usable fuel 31.6 gal.

1. Groundspeed: 110 − 15 = **95 kt**
2. En-route time: 150 ÷ 95 = **1.579 hr** (1 h 35 min)
3. Trip fuel (start, taxi, climb, cruise, descent, approach): 1.579 × 13 = **20.53 gal**
4. Reserve: 13 ÷ 3 = **4.33 gal** (20 min)
5. Minimum usable fuel at brake release: 20.53 + 4.33 = **24.86 gal** (round up to 25.0 gal)
6. Check against usable capacity: 25.0 gal ≤ 31.6 gal usable — legal, with 6.6 gal of discretionary margin.

If step 5 exceeds usable capacity, the flight cannot legally depart as planned: shorten the leg, add a fuel stop, or wait for a better wind forecast. There is no regulatory mechanism to trade the 20 minutes away.

## 6. Ramp-check / verification procedure

A deterministic pre-departure check an inspector or dispatcher can reproduce:

1. **Record usable fuel on board** at brake release (dipstick/gauges converted to gallons or pounds; use POH usable quantity).
2. **Compute trip fuel** to the first point of intended landing using forecast winds and forecast temperature (fuel to the *first* point of intended landing — not to a later point on the route).
3. **Compute reserve** = cruise burn ÷ 3 (gallons) or cruise burn × density ÷ 3 (pounds).
4. **Pass criterion:** usable fuel on board ≥ trip fuel + reserve. Any shortfall is a violation of § 91.151(b) at the moment of departure, regardless of what the flight subsequently burns.
5. **Re-apply at each departure.** The rule governs the *beginning* of a flight; each subsequent leg out of an intermediate stop gets its own trip fuel plus 20 minutes. Fuel remaining from the previous leg may be counted, but the reserve is re-established, not carried as credit.

## 7. Applicability boundaries (when the answer changes)

- **IFR instead of VFR:** § 91.167(a)(3) — helicopter 30 minutes at normal cruising speed after the alternate (or after the first airport when no alternate is required). Not the subject of this ask.
- **Non-US jurisdiction:** outside the scope; this answer is FAA-specific.
- **Aircraft flight manual, operating certificate, or company ops spec more restrictive than the regulation:** the higher requirement governs. The 20 minutes is a floor, never a ceiling; § 91.103 additionally requires the pilot to become familiar with all available information, and known delays (traffic, weather) must be accounted for on top of the 20 minutes.
- **Airplane, not rotorcraft:** 30 minutes day / 45 minutes night under § 91.151(a).

## 8. Bottom line

**20 minutes at normal cruising speed — day or night, Part 91 or Part 135 — beyond the fuel needed to reach the first point of intended landing.** Expressed in volume, that is one-third of the aircraft's hourly cruise burn: 6.67 gal at 20 gph, 5.00 gal at 15 gph, 10.0 gal at 30 gph.

question: M8
answer:
ANSWERS

1) The RFC that deprecated TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 is RFC 8996, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1" (K. Moriarty, S. Farrell; March 2021; 18 pages; DOI 10.17487/RFC8996; source: TLS WG; draft-ietf-tls-oldversions-deprecate-12). RFC 8996 is itself an Internet Best Current Practice and is part of BCP 195.

2) RFC 8996 moved the RFCs that defined those versions to Historic status. Specifically, RFC 2246 (TLS 1.0) and RFC 4346 (TLS 1.1) were "moved to Historic status."

EVIDENCE (verbatim from RFC 8996)

Abstract:
  "This document formally deprecates Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 (RFC 2246) and 1.1 (RFC 4346). Accordingly, those documents have been moved to Historic status. These versions lack support for current and recommended cryptographic algorithms and mechanisms, and various government and industry profiles of applications using TLS now mandate avoiding these old TLS versions. TLS version 1.2 became the recommended version for IETF protocols in 2008 (subsequently being obsoleted by TLS version 1.3 in 2018), providing sufficient time to transition away from older versions. Removing support for older versions from implementations reduces the attack surface, reduces opportunity for misconfiguration, and streamlines library and product maintenance."

  "This document also deprecates Datagram TLS (DTLS) version 1.0 (RFC 4347) but not DTLS version 1.2, and there is no DTLS version 1.1."

  "This document updates many RFCs that normatively refer to TLS version 1.0 or TLS version 1.1, as described herein. This document also updates the best practices for TLS usage in RFC 7525; hence, it is part of BCP 195."

Status of This Memo:
  "This memo documents an Internet Best Current Practice."

Section 1 (Introduction):
  "Transport Layer Security (TLS) versions 1.0 [RFC2246] and 1.1 [RFC4346] were superseded by TLS 1.2 [RFC5246] in 2008, which has now itself been superseded by TLS 1.3 [RFC8446]. Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS) version 1.0 [RFC4347] was superseded by DTLS 1.2 [RFC6347] in 2012. Therefore, it is timely to further deprecate TLS 1.0, TLS 1.1, and DTLS 1.0. Accordingly, the aforementioned documents have been moved to Historic status."

Technical reasons given for the deprecation (Section 1):
  - "They require the implementation of older cipher suites that are no longer desirable for cryptographic reasons, e.g., TLS 1.0 makes TLS_DHE_DSS_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA mandatory to implement."
  - "There is a lack of support for current recommended cipher suites, especially authenticated encryption with associated data (AEAD) ciphers, which were not supported prior to TLS 1.2."
  - "The integrity of the handshake depends on SHA-1 hash."
  - "The authentication of the peers depends on SHA-1 signatures."

PRECISION NOTES (things a careful reader should not conflate)

- "Status" vs. "Obsoletes". The status assigned is Historic (an IETF stream status). RFC 8996's own header lists its obsoletes as RFC 5469 and RFC 7507 only. RFC 2246 and RFC 4346 are not in RFC 8996's obsoletes list because they had already been obsoleted earlier (TLS 1.0/RFC 2246 by TLS 1.2/RFC 5246; RFC 4346 by TLS 1.3/RFC 8446); RFC 8996's action on them is the status change to Historic, plus its many "Updates" relationships.

- Per-document mapping. TLS 1.0 = RFC 2246; TLS 1.1 = RFC 4346. RFC 8996 assigns Historic to both, and additionally to DTLS 1.0 (RFC 4347) and to RFC 5469 (DES/IDEA cipher suites), which was moved to Historic "since the only versions of TLS for which their usage is defined are now Historic." DTLS 1.2 (RFC 6347) is explicitly not deprecated, though it is updated by RFC 8996 to forbid negotiating DTLS 1.0.

- Scope of the update action. RFC 8996 updates a long list of RFCs that normatively refer to TLS 1.0 or 1.1, and updates RFC 7525 (TLS best practices), which is why it is part of BCP 195. A few referenced RFCs (e.g., RFC 6460, RFC 4743, RFC 4744) were already Historic and are listed only to reiterate that obsolete-protocol usage should use modern TLS.

- Status vs. deprecation mechanism. "Deprecation" here is the formal IETF standards-track action of moving a protocol specification to Historic status; it is distinct from vendor removals, regulatory mandates (e.g., PCI DSS), or profiles that merely recommend against TLS 1.0/1.1.

- Current-state check. RFC 8996 was published 2021-03-23 (Datatracker document history) and remains the deprecating document; no later RFC in the fetched material supersedes it.

ONE-LINE ANSWER
RFC 8996, "Deprecating TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1" (BCP 195, March 2021), deprecated TLS 1.0 (RFC 2246) and TLS 1.1 (RFC 4346) by moving those RFCs to Historic status (and it also moved DTLS 1.0/RFC 4347 and RFC 5469 to Historic).

question: M10
answer:
## Answer

**The 2026 US Social Security contribution and benefit base (OASDI taxable maximum) is $184,500.**

That is the maximum amount of an individual's wages/self-employment income subject to Social Security (OASDI) payroll tax for calendar-year 2026. Earnings above $184,500 in 2026 are not subject to OASDI tax, and the same $184,500 limit is the maximum earnings creditable toward a 2026 benefit computation.

This is the official, already-announced figure — not a projection. It was published by SSA with the December 2025 cost-of-living adjustment (2.8 percent) and the 2024 national average wage index ($69,846.57).

## Source of the figure (authoritative)

- SSA, Contribution and Benefit Base table — year-by-year series shows: 2024 = $168,600; 2025 = $176,100; **2026 = $184,500**; 2027 = $192,300. (ssa.gov/oact/COLA/cbb.html)
- SSA, Detailed Calculator update instructions, verbatim: *"Contribution and benefit base for 2026: $184,500"*; also *"'Old-law' contribution and benefit base for 2026: $137,100"*; COLA for December 2025 = 2.8 percent; national average wage index for 2024 = $69,846.57. (ssa.gov/oact/anypia/update.html)
- SSA, automatic-determination method page confirms the statutory formula (1994 base of $60,600 x ratio of the NAWI for year Y-2 to the 1992 NAWI of $22,935.42, rounded to the nearest multiple of $300, never reduced) and uses $184,500 as the 2026 base against which the 2027 base ($192,300) is tested. (ssa.gov/oact/COLA/cbbdet.html)

**Do not confuse with 2027.** The $192,300 figure appearing in SSA's current lead paragraph is the **2027** base. The 2026 base is $184,500.

## Payroll application — 2026 OASDI maximum contributions

| Item | Rate | Applied to | 2026 maximum contribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| Employee OASDI | 6.2% | $184,500 | **$11,439.00** |
| Employer OASDI | 6.2% | $184,500 | **$11,439.00** |
| Combined (employee + employer) | 12.4% | $184,500 | **$22,878.00** |
| Self-employed (SECA/OASDI portion) | 12.4% | $184,500 | **$22,878.00** |

Arithmetic: 184,500 x 0.062 = 11,439.00; 184,500 x 0.124 = 22,878.00. The self-employed OASDI maximum equals the combined employee-plus-employer maximum, as it must.

Medicare (HI) is separate and has **no earnings cap** for 2026 (no HI taxable maximum has existed since 1993). The Additional Medicare Tax of 0.9% on wages over $200,000 (single)/$250,000 (MFJ) is likewise unrelated to the $184,500 base — do not apply $184,500 to Medicare withholding.

## Payroll-operations notes (how the base is applied)

1. **Annual, per-employer cumulative.** The cap is an annual dollar limit applied to cumulative taxable wages within the calendar year, not a per-payroll-period cap. There is no proration: each pay period's OASDI-taxable wages = min(period wages, 184,500 minus YTD OASDI-taxable wages). Withholding stops once YTD OASDI wages reach $184,500.
2. **No per-period equivalent exists.** $184,500 / 26 = $7,096.15 and / 24 = $7,687.50 are arithmetic artifacts only; a semimonthly employee earning $7,700 per period is not capped at $7,687.50 — the cap binds only on the cumulative annual total.
3. **Mid-year hires / wage-base changes.** Use the employee's YTD OASDI-taxable wages carried from the prior payroll provider; do not restart the $184,500 accumulator at hire.
4. **Multiple employers.** Each employer applies the full $184,500 independently. Any excess employee OASDI withheld across employers is recoverable by the employee as a refundable credit on Form 1040 — not by the employer adjusting its own returns.
5. **Employer match is not refundable.** The employer's 6.2% on wages up to $184,500 per employee is owed per employer regardless of the employee's aggregate position.
6. **Related 2026 figures that must not be substituted for the base:** "old-law" contribution and benefit base for 2026 = $137,100 (used in benefit-computation contexts, not for withholding); 2026 base = $184,500; 2027 base = $192,300.
7. **System configuration (2026 tax year):** OASDI wage base = 184,500.00; OASDI rates 6.2% EE / 6.2% ER / 12.4% SE; HI wage base = unlimited; verify the 2025-to-2026 rollover so no employee is capped at the 2025 figure of $176,100.

## Verification of internal consistency

- 2025 ($176,100) < **2026 ($184,500)** < 2027 ($192,300) — ordering holds everywhere cited above.
- Old-law 2026 base ($137,100) < 2026 base ($184,500) — consistent as a distinct benefit-computation figure.
- Contribution maxima are exactly 6.2% and 12.4% of $184,500 ($11,439.00 and $22,878.00) with no figure exceeding the stated base.
- No Medicare dollar cap is stated, because none exists — avoiding a fabricated value that would conflict with the OASDI base.

question: M12
answer:
ANSWER

The 2026 limit on an employee's elective deferrals to a 401(k) plan, before any catch-up contribution, is $24,500.

This is the IRC §402(g)(1) elective deferral limit — the cap on the combined pre-tax and designated Roth elective deferrals an employee may make across all plans in which the employee participates, measured on a calendar-year basis. It applies per employee, not per plan.

AUTHORITY

1. IRS Notice 2025-67 (the 2026 cost-of-living adjustment notice): 'The limitation under section 402(g)(1) on the exclusion for elective deferrals described in section 402(g)(3) ... is increased from $23,500 to $24,500.'
2. IRS, Retirement topics — 401(k) and profit-sharing plan contribution limits: 'The limit on employee elective deferrals (for traditional and safe harbor plans) is: $24,500 in 2026, subject to cost-of-living adjustments.'
3. IRS, Retirement topics — Contributions: 'The basic limit on elective deferrals is $24,500 in 2026, $23,500 in 2025, $23,000 in 2024 and $22,500 in 2023, or 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less.'

The figure is officially published; it does not need to be derived from the statutory indexation formula.

SCOPE AND DEFINITION NOTES (so the number is not misapplied)

- 'Before any catch-up' means the base limit only. The age-50+ catch-up for 2026 is $8,000, and the enhanced SECURE 2.0 catch-up for participants who attain age 60, 61, 62 or 63 in 2026 is $11,250. Those are added on top of the base: a participant age 50+ may defer up to $32,500 ($24,500 + $8,000), and a participant aged 60–63 up to $35,750 ($24,500 + $11,250). Those totals are outside the scope of the question and are shown only to confirm the base figure is the pre-catch-up number.
- The limit is also capped at 100% of the employee's compensation, whichever is less.
- Pre-tax and Roth (designated Roth) elective deferrals share this single $24,500 limit; designating a deferral as Roth does not create additional room.
- This is NOT the §415(c) total annual additions limit, which for 2026 is $72,000 and covers employee deferrals plus employer match, employer nonelective contributions, after-tax contributions and forfeiture allocations combined.
- This is NOT the SIMPLE 401(k) limit. For 2026 the SIMPLE 401(k)/SIMPLE IRA salary reduction limit is $17,000 (with $18,100 available under §408(p)(2)(E)(i)(I)/(II) for certain plans of small employers). A SIMPLE 401(k) is a different plan type from a standard 401(k).
- The §401(a)(17) compensation cap for 2026 is $360,000; that is a limit on compensation taken into account, not on deferrals.
- The 2027 figure is $25,500 (IRS Notice 2026-66). It is not the answer for 2026 and should not be used for 2026 payroll.

PLAN-LEVEL CAVEATS (do not change the statutory answer)

- A plan document may impose a lower deferral cap than $24,500; the statutory limit is a ceiling, not a guarantee.
- Highly compensated employees may effectively be limited below $24,500 by the ADP nondiscrimination test.
- Automatic enrollment defaults, per-payroll caps and percentage-of-pay caps are plan design features, not the §402(g) limit.

HR OPERATING GUIDANCE

- Configure 2026 payroll deferral caps at $24,500 for the base limit, with catch-up buckets of $8,000 (age 50+) and $11,250 (attains 60–63 in 2026) enabled only if the plan permits catch-up contributions.
- Apply the age-based catch-up based on the participant's age at the end of the 2026 calendar year.
- Monitor across all employer plans: if a participant defers to more than one employer's plan, the $24,500 aggregate must be tested at the participant level, and excess deferrals must be corrected (distributed by April 15, 2027 to avoid double taxation).
- Note the separate 2026 Roth catch-up rule for high earners (FICA-compensation threshold increased to $150,000 for 2026) if the plan offers catch-up contributions.

question: M2
answer:
# Current US national primary ambient air quality standards (NAAQS) for PM2.5

## 1. Answer record

| # | Averaging period | Primary level | Form / compliance convention (40 CFR part 50, App. N) | Authority |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Annual (1-year) | **9.0 µg/m³** | Annual arithmetic mean, averaged over 3 years; level defined to one decimal place | 40 CFR 50.20(a), (b) |
| 2 | 24-hour | **35 µg/m³** | Annual 98th percentile of 24-hour average concentrations, averaged over 3 years; integer level | 40 CFR 50.20(a), (c) |

Both are **primary** (health-based) standards. Units are micrograms per cubic meter of ambient air, measured as PM2.5 (aerodynamic diameter ≤ nominal 2.5 µm) by an FRM based on App. L or an FEM designated under part 53.

## 2. Regulatory basis and currency

- Codified text: **40 CFR 50.20**, "National primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5", promulgated at **89 FR 16202 (Mar. 6, 2024)**, standard text at 89 FR 16380; effective May 6, 2024 (60 days after Federal Register publication).
- Operative language, § 50.20(a): *"the national primary ambient air quality standards for PM2.5 are 9.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour average concentration ..."*
- § 50.20(b): the annual standard *"is met when the annual arithmetic mean concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N to this part, is less than or equal to 9.0 µg/m³."*
- § 50.20(c): the 24-hour standard *"is met when the 98th percentile 24-hour concentration, as determined in accordance with appendix N to this part, is less than or equal to 35 µg/m³."*
- **Verification date: 2026-11-16 (UTC).** The eCFR text of § 50.20 as of that date carries the 9.0 / 35 values with no later amendment note, so no suspension or modification of the 2024 annual level is reflected in the codified rule. "Current" is time-sensitive: the Clean Air Act requires review every 5 years; re-verify against 40 CFR 50.20 and EPA's NAAQS table before any downstream use.
- Three independent confirmations agree:
  1. eCFR § 50.20 (quoted above).
  2. EPA "Timeline of PM NAAQS" table, 2024 row (89 FR 16202, Mar. 6, 2024): primary PM2.5, 1 year, **9.0 µg/m³**, annual arithmetic mean averaged over 3 years; "All other primary and secondary PM2.5 and PM10 standards, retained without revision."
  3. EPA "PM NAAQS Overview" (Feb 2024): *"EPA is revising the level of the primary (health-based) annual PM2.5 standard from 12.0 µg/m³ to 9.0 µg/m³ ... EPA is retaining the primary 24-hour PM2.5 standard at the level of 35 µg/m³."*

## 3. Read this before citing 12.0 µg/m³

**40 CFR 50.18** also exists in the current CFR and states *"12.0 micrograms per cubic meter (µg/m³) annual arithmetic mean concentration and 35 µg/m³ 24-hour average concentration"* ([78 FR 3277, Jan. 15, 2013]). It is **not** the current annual standard. It is the 2012-revision annual level, left standing in the CFR because implementation of that standard (designations, SIP obligations, nonattainment classifications, and the associated deadlines) continues on its own timetable even after the level is superseded. § 50.20 is the operative current standard.

Practical rule: if a source returns 12.0 for the PM2.5 annual NAAQS, it is either (a) quoting § 50.18, or (b) a pre-March-2024 document. Neither is an answer to "current".

## 4. Secondary (welfare-based) standards — not asked, recorded only to prevent mixing

- Annual secondary: **15.0 µg/m³**, annual arithmetic mean averaged over 3 years.
- 24-hour secondary: **35 µg/m³**, 98th percentile averaged over 3 years (same level and form as the primary 24-hour).
- Retained without revision in the 2024 primary review and again in the Dec. 27, 2024 action (89 FR 105692) covering the secondary PM2.5 and PM10 standards.
- § 50.7 in the CFR holds the primary-and-secondary PM2.5 standards from the 1997/2006 actions; it is not the current primary annual level either.

## 5. Compliance and rounding conventions (needed to apply the levels correctly)

- **Annual:** compare the 3-year average of annual means to 9.0, rounded to one decimal place. 9.04 → 9.0 → **meets**; 9.05 → 9.1 → **violates**.
- **24-hour:** compare the 3-year average of annual 98th percentiles to 35, rounded to a whole number. 35.49 → 35 → **meets**; 35.50 → 36 → **violates**.
- The compared quantity is the site's **design value (DV)**, computed per 40 CFR part 50 App. N: the "annual PM2.5 NAAQS DV" and the "24-hour (or daily) PM2.5 NAAQS DV".
- Only FRM/FEM measurements deemed "suitable" under part 58, and only eligible sites (per §§ 58.11 / 58.30 for the annual standard; § 58.11 for the 24-hour standard), enter the computation.
- Data influenced by exceptional events may be excluded only through the § 50.14 process.

## 6. One-line answer for direct citation

> Primary PM2.5 NAAQS, current as of 2026-11-16: **9.0 µg/m³ annual** (arithmetic mean, 3-year average) and **35 µg/m³ 24-hour** (98th percentile, 3-year average), per 40 CFR 50.20 as revised in the 2024 PM NAAQS review, 89 FR 16202 (Mar. 6, 2024).

## 7. Source list

1. 40 CFR 50.20 — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-50/section-50.20 (fetched 2026-11-16T06:31:33Z, sha256 1350a153e535).
2. 40 CFR 50.18 (superseded 2012 annual level) — https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-40/chapter-I/subchapter-C/part-50/section-50.18 (fetched 2026-11-16T06:31:33Z, sha256 7cf2e727c2ee).
3. EPA, Timelines of PM NAAQS — https://www.epa.gov/pm-pollution/timeline-particulate-matter-pm-national-ambient-air-quality-standards-naaqs (fetched 2026-11-16T06:31:32Z).
4. EPA, PM NAAQS Overview (Feb 2024) — https://www.epa.gov/system/files/documents/2024-02/pm-naaqs-overview.pdf (fetched 2026-11-16T06:31:33Z).
5. 40 CFR part 50 App. N (data handling / DV definitions) — CFR 2025 title 40 vol. 2, govinfo.gov PDF (fetched 2026-11-16T06:31:33Z).
